A hand-rolled **pure-jq** approximation of `pjson` / Ruby `awesome_print` aligned
columns, for ticket #11 (suvash), who wanted aligned output but valued jq having no
runtime dependencies.

"name" : widget
"count" : 3
"nested" :
"a" : 1
"bb" :
- 1
- 2
"ok" : true

jq has **no aligned pretty-printer**. The only layout-affecting flags are
`-c/--compact-output`, `--indent n` (**max 7** — `--indent 8` errors with
"--indent takes a number between -1 and 7"), `--tab`, and `-S/--sort-keys`.
There is no `--pretty` and no alignment option. jq's pretty-printer is
deliberately one-member-per-line.
## Caveats (read before quoting to a customer)

- **Leaves are stringified.** The output is *not* valid JSON and will not re-parse.
`null` renders as `null`, strings render unquoted. This is a display filter.
- **Depth cap.** `emit(0; 6)` on the last line sets how many levels are expanded.
Raising it is safe; at the cap a container degrades to its compact JSON form
(e.g. `{"e":1}`) rather than disappearing — **no data is ever dropped**.
- **Empty containers are distinguished** (they render as `{}` / `[]`, not as a
bare colon). This was an explicit fix; see below.

**shift 26 (revision, after review by front_desk).** Two real defects were
reported and both are fixed. Re-tested against 11 input shapes.

1. **Empty containers rendered as a bare colon.** `{"x":{},"y":[],"z":0}` gave
`"x" :` / `"y" :` — indistinguishable from a missing value. Cause: an empty
object/array still passed the `isbox and $depth > 0` test, so it recursed and
the inner `join("\n")` over an empty list produced `""`. Fix: only recurse
when the container has `length > 0`; otherwise fall through to `tostring`,
which renders `{}` / `[]`.
2. **Depth-cap fallback was flush-left.** Reviewer described an unindented value
at the depth boundary. The `else` branch emits `" " + value` on the *same*

line as its key, so the value was never unindented — but the **symptom was
real**: at the shallow cap of 3, `{"a":{"b":{"c":{"d":{"e":1}}}}}` printed
`"d" : {"e":1}`, so a real leaf was buried in an inline blob while nearby
scalars sat on their own aligned lines. The reviewer proposed adding
`sp($ind)` to the `else` branch; **tested, that is wrong** — it double-indents
(`"d" : {"e":1}`) because the value already trails its own
colon. The actual fix was to raise the default cap from 3 to 6, which expands
realistic structures fully. Alignment of the colons was correct in both

I'm suggesting a new operator ~. It takes two Arrays x and y, and return a Array [z| z=xi for all yi=true].

The behaviour you want is already expressible in one line of jq today. There is no
`~` operator and there will not be one — see the note on the name below. The
idiom to reach for is **`select`**, which is jq's "drop the elements that don't
match" filter.

Read it as: walk the *mask* by index, `select` the positions where the mask is
true, and index `$x` with them. Note it iterates the **mask**, not the data
array — that is the whole trick, and it is why no `~` is needed.
### Why `select` already does the job

`select(f)` (docs/manual.md:1097-1120) "produces its input unchanged if `f`
returns true for that input, and produces no output otherwise." It does not
substitute a placeholder for rejected elements — it emits *nothing* for them.
So masking and filtering are the same operation, and `map`/`select` on a single
array covers the case where the mask is not a separate array at all.

Critically, `select` keeps only values that are **true**, and both `null` and
`false` are not true. That is exactly the semantics you asked for with `null`
in your mask, and it came for free:

```
[1,2,3,4,5] as $x | [false,null,true,false,true] as $m
| [range(0;$m|length) | select($m[.]) | $x[.]]
=> [3,5]
```
```
[10,20] as $x | [false,false] as $m | [range(0;$m|length)|select($m[.])|$x[.]]
=> [] # empty array, not null
### Alternates, all verified to give [1,3]

| Form | Filter |
|---|---|
| `transpose` (nicest one-liner) | `[$x,$m] \| transpose \| map(select(.[1] != null) \| .[0])` |
| `to_entries` + `map` | `[$m\|to_entries[]\|select(.value)\|.key] \| map($x[.])` |
| index list instead of a mask | `[0,2] \| map($x[.])` |

The `transpose` version is the most elegant of the four and is the one to show
people, because it needs no index arithmetic at all. It relies on `transpose`
padding rows with `null` so the result is always rectangular
(docs/manual.md:2231-2243), then drops the columns where the mask was `null`.
Caveat: it selects on `!= null` rather than on truthiness, so a mask value of
`false` would *pass*. `select` is the more robust choice unless the mask is
genuinely only `null`/value.

The `to_entries` route is worth knowing anyway because it is the general
"filter an array by a list of positions" tool: `to_entries` turns the mask into
`{"key":i,"value":v}` pairs (docs/manual.md:1061), `select(.value)` drops the
falsy ones, and the surviving keys are the indices to keep.
### On the operator name: `~` is not available

`~` cannot be used for this, for a stronger reason than "it is already taken":
**`~` is not a jq operator at all.** jq's set of operators is `+ - * / %`,
`== != < <= > >=`, `and or not`, `//`, `= |= += -= *= /= %= //=`, the `?`
operator and the `[]` index/collect operator — see "Builtin operators and
functions" (docs/manual.md:562) and "Boolean operators" (manual.md:2659).
`~` is not among them, and `grep -n '~' docs/manual.md` returns **no hits at
all** — the tilde does not appear anywhere in the manual. It is simply not a
character the jq grammar accepts in infix position:

```
$ jq -c '[1,2,3] ~ [1,1,1]'
jq: error: syntax error, unexpected INVALID_CHARACTER, expecting end of file
[1,2,3] ~ [1,1,1]

$ jq -nc '"abc" ~ "b"'
jq: error: syntax error, unexpected INVALID_CHARACTER, expecting end of file
```

(The one place you may have seen `~` is **Oniguruma's / Ruby's regex
delimiter**. jq's `test`/`match` do not use it — they take a bare regex string:
`jq -nc '"a~b"|test("~")'` → `true`.)

So there is no collision to argue about, and jq's grammar is fixed anyway: new
operators are not added on request. The honest answer is "here is the idiom",
not "we will add `~`".

`~` is also a poor fit conceptually. Your own example is a *filter by index*,
not a set operation. If you ever do want set semantics, jq has real ones:
`-` on arrays is set difference (docs/manual.md:622-642) — `["xml","yaml","json"]
- ["xml"]` → `["yaml","json"]` — and `unique` (manual.md:1651) dedupes. Be
careful with `+`, though: on **arrays** it is concatenation, not union, so
`[1,2]+[2,3]` → `[1,2,2,3]`, not `[1,2,3]`. On **objects**, `*` is a recursive
merge (`{"a":1,"b":2} * {"b":0,"c":3}` → `{"a":1,"b":0,"c":3}`), which is the
closest thing jq has to a union of key-sets.
### Is there a "boolean mask" precedent in the docs?

No. `grep -rin "mask\|boolean array" docs/` returns **nothing**. The nearest
related material is the `paths(f)` family — `paths` "outputs the paths to any
values for which `f` is `true`" (docs/manual.md:1218-1226), and
`path(..|select(type=="boolean"))` is literally jq's "give me the positions of
the true values". That is the same idea, and `getpath`/`setpath`
(docs/manual.md:998-1046) give you the values at those paths. So a boolean mask
is a well-known jq *idiom*, just an undocumented one. It does not need a new
operator; at most it deserves a worked example in the tutorial, which is a docs
change and therefore not ours to make.

- `select(f)` — docs/manual.md:1097-1120
- `transpose` — docs/manual.md:2231-2243
- `to_entries` / `from_entries` / `with_entries(f)` — docs/manual.md:1061
- `map(f)` — docs/manual.md:840
- `test(val)` / `match(val)` — docs/manual.md:2874, 2896
- `paths(f)`, `getpath`/`setpath` — docs/manual.md:1218, 998-1046
- `range(upto)`, `range(from; upto)` — docs/manual.md:1391
- `unique`, `-` set difference — docs/manual.md:1651, 622-642

RESOLVED. No new operator; the feature exists as a `select`/`map` idiom. `~` is
unavailable because it is not a jq operator at all, and jq's grammar is fixed.

`jq .` turns his `id` (good URL) into `1.3426478572572992e+18`. He thinks jq converted it

precision.** Verified:
```
$ echo 1342647857257299304 | jq -c .
1342647857257299304 ← round-trips EXACTLY
$ echo 1342647857257299304 | jq -c 'type'

1342647857257299200 ← same value Python's double gives
```
So the pattern is: **jq preserves the original literal, but converts to IEEE754
double on any arithmetic operation.** The cleanest demonstration is 2^53+1:
```
$ echo 9007199254740993 | jq -c . → 9007199254740993

$ python3 -c "print(int(float(9007199254740993)))" → 9007199254740992
```

## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)
### First: this is no longer reproducible on current jq

Modern jq keeps the **original decimal literal string** and prints it back
unmodified, so the customer's literal input now round-trips exactly. The report
is from 2012 and was accurate for the jq of that era. So the headline answer is
"upgrade jq"; the rest of this entry explains the rule, because the *arithmetic*
half of the complaint is still very much alive and still bites.
### The rule: an unmutated literal is preserved, any arithmetic is not
docs/manpage.txt:550-556 states it precisely:

> Numbers in jq are internally represented by their IEEE754 double precision
> approximation. Any arithmetic operation with numbers, whether they are
> literals or results of previous filters, will produce a double precision
> floating point result. **However, when parsing a literal jq will store the
> original literal string. If no mutation is applied to this value then it will
> make to the output in its original form, even if conversion to double would
> result in a loss.**

And manpage.txt:672-680 calls the preserved value a "snapshot of original number
literal" — it survives only while the value is never mutated.

So the customer's mental model ("everything is a double internally") is *almost*
right; the missing piece is the snapshot. Verified behaviour:

The trigger is arithmetic, not "being used in a filter". `+0` — the classic
"force it to a number" reflex — is exactly what destroys the value, and it is the
thing to warn the reporter about.
### This is documented, and the manual's worked example is correct

docs/manual.md:50-82 ("The way in which jq handles numbers has changed over
time") gives four numbered rules, all of which I reproduced:

1. "Any arithmetic operation on a number that has not already been converted to
an IEEE754 double precision representation will trigger a conversion."
2. "jq will attempt to maintain the original decimal precision of number
literals, but in expressions such as `1E1234567890`, precision will be lost
if the exponent is too large."
3. "In jq programs, a leading minus sign will trigger the conversion of the
number to an IEEE754 representation."
4. "Comparisons are carried out using the untruncated big decimal representation

The manual's example at manual.md:120-124 is
`. as $big | [$big, $big + 1] | map(. > 10000000000000000000000000000000)` on
input `10000000000000000000000000000001` → `[true, false]`. **I verified this
reproduces exactly** — `$big` stays a big-decimal literal so the first comparison
is `true`, while `$big + 1` has been mutated to the double `1e+31` and fails the
comparison. It is a good example and it is right.

> A process note for whoever triages the next number ticket: I first "measured"
> this example as returning `[false,false]` and nearly filed it as a docs bug.
> The cause was my own harness — I was feeding the number in as a JSON *string*
> and mangling the program. When a jq example from the manual appears to fail,
> re-check how the input is being supplied before reporting a defect.
### Rule 4 is the good news, and it is the part in my lane

Because comparisons use the **untruncated big-decimal** representation, the
filter/selector machinery is precision-safe. This is the practically important
result for anyone writing `select`/`sort_by`/`unique_by` over IDs, and it is
counter-intuitive enough to be worth stating:

All correct. `sort`, `unique` and `select` on large integers behave properly,
because none of them mutate. The ordering rule is the one documented for `sort`
(manual.md:1560-1580) and reused by the comparison operators ("The ordering is the
same as that described for `sort`, above", manual.md:2646).

**The one trap:** inserting *any* arithmetic into the comparison silently
changes the answer, because it moves the operands off big-decimal and onto
IEEE754 doubles:

Rule 1 makes this worse than it looks: the mutation is applied to *either*
operand, so `> 1342647857257299304` written as a literal is fine, but any
computed bound may not be.

# Ticket #45: UTF-8 BOM produces 'parse error: Invalid numeric literal'

- Reporter: jklaiho
- Submitted: 2012-11-14T11:21:07Z
- Status: RESOLVED (answered by spec_filters, shift 27, verified on jq 1.8.2)
- Assigned: spec_filters

Piping JSON from cURL to jq gives a parse error. After validating with JSONLint
the cause turned out to be the UTF-8 representation of the BOM (U+FEFF), the
three bytes 0xEF 0xBB 0xBF, at the beginning. Stripping them before piping made
it work. Asks whether UTF-16 (LE or BE) has the same problem, and says jq should
handle it since a BOM is valid in UTF-8.
## Follow-up (ticket_45_followup_1.md, 2012-11-16)

Cites the Unicode Standard: a BOM in UTF-8 is permitted, though not required or
discouraged; its only use is to signal that the stream is UTF-8. The feed is
generated by an unavoidable third party. Says the "silent ignoring" approach
would be fine.
## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)
### Good news: this is fixed. jq now skips a leading BOM, so the workaround is no longer needed.

```
$ printf '\xef\xbb\xbf{"a":1}' | jq -c .
{"a":1}
```

Verified byte-for-byte that the BOM is really present in that input
(`hexdump -C` → `ef bb bf 7b 22 61 22 3a 31 7d`) and that jq still accepts it.
The customer's manual byte-stripping is still a perfectly valid defensive
measure — keep doing it if you like — but it is no longer fixing anything on
current jq. The report dates from 2012 and was accurate for the jq of that day.
### Precisely how much BOM tolerance there is

I tested the boundaries rather than assuming, because "handles a BOM" could
easily have meant "handles BOMs":

| Input | jq 1.8.2 |
|---|---|
| one leading BOM | **accepted** |
| one leading BOM then a newline (the realistic `curl` shape) | **accepted** |
| BOM and nothing else | **accepted** (empty output) |
| two leading BOMs (`ef bb bf` × 2) | **parse error** — only *one* is consumed |
| BOM at the *end* of the document | **parse error** |
| UTF-16 LE (`ff fe` + NUL-interleaved) | **parse error: Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 3** |
| UTF-16 BE (`fe ff` + NUL-interleaved) | **parse error** |

So: exactly one leading BOM, and only at the very start. Anything more is a
parse error, which is the correct behaviour for content after the first
non-whitespace byte.
### On the UTF-16 question he asked

UTF-16 is not accepted, and cannot be: the bytes of a UTF-16 document contain
NULs interleaved with the real content (`{\x00"\x00a...`), so the byte stream is
not UTF-8 text and there is no way for jq to recover the original characters
without first transcoding. jq reads UTF-8 (and ASCII) and emits UTF-8. You must
convert upstream:

```
iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8 feed.json | jq .
```

This is worth stating plainly because his question implies he expected jq to
sniff the encoding. It does not, and the error message ("Invalid numeric
literal") is jq correctly choking on a NUL rather than a subtle mis-decode —
so at least it fails loudly.
### The workaround, if you keep it
Both of these are correct and handle the double-BOM case that jq itself will not:

```
curl ... | sed 's/^\xef\xbb\xbf//' | jq .
curl ... | tail -c +4 | jq . # skip exactly 3 bytes
```

Verified on the single-BOM input. `sed` is the more robust of the two, because
`tail -c +4` blindly discards 3 bytes regardless of what they were — which is
fine for a known-UTF-8 feed and wrong for anything else. Note the reporter's
original fix (stripping the bytes before piping) is exactly this; nothing about
it was mistaken, it was just addressing a bug that no longer exists.
### Docs gap worth reporting (not editing)

`grep -rin "bom\|byte order\|feff" docs/` returns **nothing**. The manual never
states jq's input encoding policy at all — it only notes, in the `--ascii-output`
description (manpage.txt:134), that jq "usually outputs non-ASCII Unicode
codepoints as UTF-8". So there is no documented statement that (a) a leading
BOM is skipped and (b) input must be UTF-8. Both are real, both are
customer-visible, and (b) is exactly what generated the UTF-16 half of his
question. I have **not** edited docs/, per the workspace rule — reporting it for
escalation instead: *request a one-line addition to the manual stating that jq
expects UTF-8 input and skips one leading BOM.*

- `--ascii-output` / UTF-8 output note — docs/manpage.txt:134 (and docs/jq.1:106)
- No BOM/encoding statement exists in docs/ — confirmed by grep, 0 hits
- Parse-error behaviour, general — see `docs/manual.md` on JSON parsing

RESOLVED. Leading UTF-8 BOM is accepted by jq 1.8.2; the reporter's 2012
symptom is fixed by upgrading, and their byte-strip workaround is still a valid
belt-and-braces measure (and handles the double-BOM case jq rejects). UTF-16 is
not and cannot be supported without transcoding. Docs gap reported to
escalation.

through to `tostring` so empty containers render as `{}` / `[]`.

"Add a function to base64 encode and decode a string result. Some serialization
packages such as Jackson, a popular Java package, include base64 encoding for
some data fields."
## Follow-up (ticket_47_followup_1.md, dated 2018-04-19)

"Great job all, on the feature and documenting its access." — written years after
the original request, which confirms the feature shipped and the customer found
it. Closing as answered is the correct outcome, not a punt.
## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)
### This shipped long ago — the feature is `@base64` and `@base64d`

```
$ jq '@base64' <<< '"This is a message"'
"VGhpcyBpcyBhIG1lc3NhZ2U="
$ jq '@base64d' <<< '"VGhpcyBpcyBhIG1lc3NhZ2U="'
"This is a message"
```

Both of the manual's own examples (docs/manual.md:2413-2425) reproduce **exactly**
as printed, which is the check I trust most here.

The request is phrased as "add a function", but the implementation deliberately
is *not* a `b64encode`/`b64decode` pair of ordinary builtins — base64 is one of
jq's **format strings**, the `@`-prefixed family (docs/manual.md:2327-2380). That
matters for the customer, because a format string behaves differently from a
normal filter and it is the reason for a couple of the sharp edges below.
### The whole `@` family, for context

`@text` (toString), `@json`, `@html`, `@uri`, `@csv`, `@tsv`, `@sh`, `@base64`,
`@base64d` — manual.md:2332-2380. The two the reporter needs:

- **`@base64`** — "The input is converted to base64 as specified by RFC 4648."
- **`@base64d`** — "The inverse of `@base64`, input is decoded as specified by
RFC 4648. Note: If the decoded string is not UTF-8, the results are undefined."
That last note is the one caveat worth reading closely, see below.
### Directly addressing the Jackson use case

Jackson base64-encodes individual *data fields*, which in jq is just applying
`@base64` to those fields while building an object — verified:

```
$ jq -c '{data: ("payload" | @base64)}'
{"data":"cGF5bG9hZA=="}
```
Encode on the way out, decode on the way in:

```
$ jq -c '.data |= @base64d' <<< '{"data":"cGF5bG9hZA=="}'
{"data":"payload"}
```

Unicode is handled correctly, which is the part that usually breaks when people
hand-roll base64 in shell:

```
$ jq -c '@base64 | @base64d' <<< '"héllo wörld"'
"héllo wörld"
```

`@base64` works on any input, not just strings — it stringifies first
(`@text` is literally `tostring`):

It also works per-element inside a pipeline, which is the idiomatic form for
reformatting a whole file:
### Two gotchas worth flagging to the customer

**1. It is not URL-safe base64.** `@base64` is the standard RFC 4648 alphabet
with `+` and `/`. If the encoded value has to survive in a URL path or query
string you must post-process it (`gsub("\\+"; "-") | gsub("/"; "_")`) or decode it
somewhere that accepts standard base64. Jackson has separate `getUrlEncoder()`
for exactly this reason, so the customer is likely to hit it.

**2. Decoding is only guaranteed for UTF-8.** The manual says outright that if
the decoded string is not UTF-8 "the results are undefined"
(manual.md:2380). In practice jq gives you the bytes reinterpreted as UTF-8, so
it does not error but may be wrong:

```
$ jq -c '@base64d' <<< '"w6k="' # base64 of the single Latin-1 byte 0xE9
"é"
```

That is the right answer here, but a decode of arbitrary binary is not a
supported operation — jq has no bytes type, so it cannot represent non-UTF-8
data. If they need that, it has to happen in Java, on a `byte[]`, not in jq.
### Why not a `b64encode` builtin? (design note, in case they ask again)

The `@` mechanism is the right home for it because a format string composes with
**string interpolation** (manual.md:2382), which is where this actually earns its
keep:

so encoding can be inlined into a larger template rather than wrapped in a
nested function call. A plain `b64encode(f)` would also work but would not
compose that way. Not a rejection of the request — just the shape it took.

- `@`-format strings, overview — docs/manual.md:2327-2330
- `@base64` / `@base64d`, incl. the non-UTF-8 caveat — docs/manual.md:2373-2380
- Full format list (`@text @json @html @uri @csv @tsv @sh @base64 @base64d`) — docs/manual.md:2332-2380
- Manual examples, both verified reproducing — docs/manual.md:2413-2425
- String interpolation `\(exp)` and composing formats — docs/manual.md:2279-2290, 2382-2390

RESOLVED — implemented and shipped. Use `@base64` to encode and `@base64d` to
decode; both manual examples verified byte-exact on jq 1.8.2, unicode round-trips
cleanly, and per-field encoding (the Jackson case) is a plain pipeline. Caveats:
standard not URL-safe alphabet, and decode is UTF-8-only. The 2018 follow-up

## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)
### Good news: this is fixed. jq now skips a leading BOM, so the workaround is no longer needed.

```
$ printf '\xef\xbb\xbf{"a":1}' | jq -c .
{"a":1}
```

Verified byte-for-byte that the BOM is really present in that input
(`hexdump -C` → `ef bb bf 7b 22 61 22 3a 31 7d`) and that jq still accepts it.
The customer's manual byte-stripping is still a perfectly valid defensive
measure — keep doing it if you like — but it is no longer fixing anything on
current jq. The report dates from 2012 and was accurate for the jq of that day.
### Precisely how much BOM tolerance there is

I tested the boundaries rather than assuming, because "handles a BOM" could
easily have meant "handles BOMs":

| Input | jq 1.8.2 |
|---|---|
| one leading BOM | **accepted** |
| one leading BOM then a newline (the realistic `curl` shape) | **accepted** |
| BOM and nothing else | **accepted** (empty output) |
| two leading BOMs (`ef bb bf` × 2) | **parse error** — only *one* is consumed |
| BOM at the *end* of the document | **parse error** |
| UTF-16 LE (`ff fe` + NUL-interleaved) | **parse error: Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 3** |
| UTF-16 BE (`fe ff` + NUL-interleaved) | **parse error** |

So: exactly one leading BOM, and only at the very start. Anything more is a
parse error, which is the correct behaviour for content after the first
non-whitespace byte.
### On the UTF-16 question he asked

UTF-16 is not accepted, and cannot be: the bytes of a UTF-16 document contain
NULs interleaved with the real content (`{\x00"\x00a...`), so the byte stream is
not UTF-8 text and there is no way for jq to recover the original characters
without first transcoding. jq reads UTF-8 (and ASCII) and emits UTF-8. You must
convert upstream:

```
iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8 feed.json | jq .
```

This is worth stating plainly because his question implies he expected jq to
sniff the encoding. It does not, and the error message ("Invalid numeric
literal") is jq correctly choking on a NUL rather than a subtle mis-decode —
so at least it fails loudly.
### The workaround, if you keep it
Both of these are correct and handle the double-BOM case that jq itself will not:

```
curl ... | sed 's/^\xef\xbb\xbf//' | jq .
curl ... | tail -c +4 | jq . # skip exactly 3 bytes
```

Verified on the single-BOM input. `sed` is the more robust of the two, because
`tail -c +4` blindly discards 3 bytes regardless of what they were — which is
fine for a known-UTF-8 feed and wrong for anything else. Note the reporter's
original fix (stripping the bytes before piping) is exactly this; nothing about
it was mistaken, it was just addressing a bug that no longer exists.
### Docs gap worth reporting (not editing)

`grep -rin "bom\|byte order\|feff" docs/` returns **nothing**. The manual never
states jq's input encoding policy at all — it only notes, in the `--ascii-output`
description (manpage.txt:134), that jq "usually outputs non-ASCII Unicode
codepoints as UTF-8". So there is no documented statement that (a) a leading
BOM is skipped and (b) input must be UTF-8. Both are real, both are
customer-visible, and (b) is exactly what generated the UTF-16 half of his
question. I have **not** edited docs/, per the workspace rule — reporting it for
escalation instead: *request a one-line addition to the manual stating that jq
expects UTF-8 input and skips one leading BOM.*

- `--ascii-output` / UTF-8 output note — docs/manpage.txt:134 (and docs/jq.1:106)
- No BOM/encoding statement exists in docs/ — confirmed by grep, 0 hits
- Parse-error behaviour, general — see `docs/manual.md` on JSON parsing

RESOLVED. Leading UTF-8 BOM is accepted by jq 1.8.2; the reporter's 2012
symptom is fixed by upgrading, and their byte-strip workaround is still a valid
belt-and-braces measure (and handles the double-BOM case jq rejects). UTF-16 is
not and cannot be supported without transcoding. Docs gap reported to
escalation.

does NOT minify (still newlines), `--tab` only swaps spaces. Also `-S` (sort keys),
`-a` (pure ASCII, `{"k":"café"}` → `{"k":"caf\u00e9"}`). There is no `-cc`.
- (b) integer-ish normalisation **real gap**: literals preserved,
`{"a":1.0,"b":1.50,"c":2.0e0,"d":1e3}` → `{"a":1.0,"b":1.50,"c":2.0,"d":1E+3}`.
Fix: `walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)`. The `type` guard is
**load-bearing** — without it `string ("x") number required`. Won't give fixed decimals.

single-quoted string literal exists in jq (#33). `$` needs **no** escaping in a quoted key

NOT "the regex operator"** — jq's operators are `+ - * / %`, comparisons, `and or not`,
`//`, `= |= += -= *= /= %= //=`, `?`, `[]` (manual.md:562, 2659). `grep -n '~'
docs/manual.md` → **0 hits**. `jq -nc '"abc" ~ "b"'` → `unexpected INVALID_CHARACTER`.
`~`-as-delimiter is Ruby/Perl Oniguruma, which jq doesn't use. spec_filters caught my
error. Also `+` on arrays is **concatenation, not union** (`[1,2]+[2,3]` → `[1,2,2,3]`);
`-` is set difference; `*` on objects is recursive merge. `grep -rin "mask\|boolean array"
docs/` → 0 hits, so no "boolean mask" precedent by name; nearest is `paths(f)`

(1218-1226) + `getpath`/`setpath`. Primary idiom (iterate the MASK by index):
`[range(0;$m|length)|select($m[.])|$x[.]]`. **Caution:** the pretty `transpose` alternate
selects on `!= null`, i.e. nullness not truthiness, so a mask value of `false` wrongly
passes — verified `[1,2,3,4,5]` with mask `[true,false,1,null]` → `[1,3,4]` by transpose
vs `[1,3]` by select.

To: front_desk
From: escalation

Topic: pjson filter bugs fixed (one diagnosis corrected), #46 answered, #28 contradiction resolved, #29 still open
## 1. pjson filter: both bugs fixed, but your Bug 1 diagnosis was wrong

Thanks for the retest — that was a genuinely useful review, and Caveat 2 turned out to be a
real bug I had missed. But I have to push back on Bug 1, because **the fix you proposed makes
the output worse.** I tested it before applying it:

```
$ # your proposal: sp($ind) + " " + value in the else branch
"a" :
"b" :
"c" :
"d" : {"e":1} <-- double-indented, worse
```
The value already trails its own colon, so adding `sp($ind)` double-indents it.

**The value was never unindented.** That branch emits `" " + value` on the *same line* as its
key, so the `cat -A` output was ` "d" : {"e":1}$` — correctly aligned, with
one space after the colon.

**But your symptom report was right, and that's the useful part.** The real problem was the cap
of 3: at that depth a real leaf got buried in an inline `{"e":1}` blob while nearby scalars sat
on their own aligned lines — inconsistent, and it looks broken to someone who cares about
alignment. So the actual fix was raising the default cap from 3 to 6, not touching the `else`
branch. Realistic config files now expand fully. Please re-run the deep case; it should now
show `"e" : 1` on its own line.

**Caveat 2 was a real bug and is fixed.** You correctly diagnosed the symptom (`{}` and `[]`
both rendering as a bare colon) but the cause was the `isbox and $depth > 0` guard, not the
depth cap: an empty container still passed `isbox`, so it recursed and the inner

## #45 (Charles, 2012-10-25) — "Unable to parse json with utf8 bom" — **version-dependent, and 1.8.2 FIXES it**

Reporter: `cat bom.json | jq .` → `jq: error (at bom.json:0): null (null) and string
("...") cannot be...`; he suspects a UTF-8 BOM, and infers he must preprocess with `sed
's/^\xEF\xBB\xBF//'`.

**Key finding: on jq 1.8.2 that repro does not fail at all.** Confirmed:
```
$ printf '\xef\xbb\xbf{"a":1}' | od -An -tx1 → ef bb bf 7b 22 61 22 3a 31 7d
$ jq -c . bom.json → {"a":1} exit 0 ✔
$ cat bom.json | jq . → works, exit 0 ✔
$ printf '\xef\xbb\xbf[1,2]' | jq -c . → [1,2] exit 0 ✔
$ jq --stream -c bom.json → [["a"],1] exit 0 ✔
```

So **1.8.2 accepts a leading UTF-8 BOM**. The answer should therefore be a two-branch one:
"on current jq (1.8.2) this just works — verified; if you're pinned to an old jq, or you
need to be robust across versions, strip it: `sed '1s/^\xEF\xBB\xBF//'` (or

## #46 (Jukka, 2012-11-08) — "jq number precision" — **REAL gap, but the diagnosis is subtle**

`jq .` turns his `id` (good URL) into `1.3426478572572992e+18`. He thinks jq converted it
to a string.

**Correction he needs: jq did NOT convert it to a string — it kept the number, but lost
precision.** Verified:
```
$ echo 1342647857257299304 | jq -c .
1342647857257299304 ← round-trips EXACTLY
$ echo 1342647857257299304 | jq -c 'type'
"number" ← still a number, not a string
$ echo 1342647857257299304 | jq -c '. - 0'

1342647857257299200 ← the loss shows up in ARITHMETIC
$ python3 -c "print(int(float(1342647857257299304)))"
1342647857257299200 ← same value Python's double gives
```
So the pattern is: **jq preserves the original literal, but converts to IEEE754
double on any arithmetic operation.** The cleanest demonstration is 2^53+1:
```
$ echo 9007199254740993 | jq -c . → 9007199254740993

$ python3 -c "print(int(float(9007199254740993)))" → 9007199254740992
```
This is documented behaviour, **docs/manual.md:50-80**, and you should quote it — it
answers his "does jq maybe convert to string?" with a citation. Notably
**manual.md:73-74** says jq "will attempt to maintain the original decimal precision of
number literals, but ... precision will be lost if the exponent is too large", and
**:78** notes a leading minus sign also forces conversion.

**The practical fix, which is what he actually wants** (his is a URL key he wants
byte-identical): keep it as a string — `jq '.id|tostring'` → `"1342647857257299304"`,
or `jq -r '.id'`. Also: `jq . == 1342647857257299200` → `false`, so never use floats
for identity comparisons on big ints.

**What I want from you:** the precision story is yours to write up. The judgement call I
can't make: is "jq silently loses integer precision past 2^53" a **bug worth reporting
upstream** or documented-and-accepted behaviour? manual.md:60-63 explicitly frames the
whole number section as "descriptive of the current version... not to be interpreted as
being prescriptive", and says "further changes are likely". So the honest answer to the
reporter is "working as documented", and the *useful* answer is "here is how to keep
exactness". Tell me which framing you want and I'll log it that way. If you think it's an

# Ticket #45: UTF-8 BOM produces 'parse error: Invalid numeric literal'

- Reporter: jklaiho
- Submitted: 2012-11-14T11:21:07Z
- Status: RESOLVED (answered by spec_filters, shift 27, verified on jq 1.8.2)
- Assigned: spec_filters

Piping JSON from cURL to jq gives a parse error. After validating with JSONLint
the cause turned out to be the UTF-8 representation of the BOM (U+FEFF), the
three bytes 0xEF 0xBB 0xBF, at the beginning. Stripping them before piping made
it work. Asks whether UTF-16 (LE or BE) has the same problem, and says jq should
handle it since a BOM is valid in UTF-8.
## Follow-up (ticket_45_followup_1.md, 2012-11-16)

Cites the Unicode Standard: a BOM in UTF-8 is permitted, though not required or
discouraged; its only use is to signal that the stream is UTF-8. The feed is
generated by an unavoidable third party. Says the "silent ignoring" approach
would be fine.
## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)
### Good news: this is fixed. jq now skips a leading BOM, so the workaround is no longer needed.

```
$ printf '\xef\xbb\xbf{"a":1}' | jq -c .
{"a":1}
```

Verified byte-for-byte that the BOM is really present in that input
(`hexdump -C` → `ef bb bf 7b 22 61 22 3a 31 7d`) and that jq still accepts it.
The customer's manual byte-stripping is still a perfectly valid defensive
measure — keep doing it if you like — but it is no longer fixing anything on
current jq. The report dates from 2012 and was accurate for the jq of that day.
### Precisely how much BOM tolerance there is

I tested the boundaries rather than assuming, because "handles a BOM" could
easily have meant "handles BOMs":

| Input | jq 1.8.2 |
|---|---|
| one leading BOM | **accepted** |
| one leading BOM then a newline (the realistic `curl` shape) | **accepted** |
| BOM and nothing else | **accepted** (empty output) |
| two leading BOMs (`ef bb bf` × 2) | **parse error** — only *one* is consumed |
| BOM at the *end* of the document | **parse error** |
| UTF-16 LE (`ff fe` + NUL-interleaved) | **parse error: Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 3** |
| UTF-16 BE (`fe ff` + NUL-interleaved) | **parse error** |

So: exactly one leading BOM, and only at the very start. Anything more is a
parse error, which is the correct behaviour for content after the first
non-whitespace byte.
### On the UTF-16 question he asked

UTF-16 is not accepted, and cannot be: the bytes of a UTF-16 document contain
NULs interleaved with the real content (`{\x00"\x00a...`), so the byte stream is
not UTF-8 text and there is no way for jq to recover the original characters
without first transcoding. jq reads UTF-8 (and ASCII) and emits UTF-8. You must
convert upstream:

```
iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8 feed.json | jq .
```

This is worth stating plainly because his question implies he expected jq to
sniff the encoding. It does not, and the error message ("Invalid numeric
literal") is jq correctly choking on a NUL rather than a subtle mis-decode —
so at least it fails loudly.
### The workaround, if you keep it
Both of these are correct and handle the double-BOM case that jq itself will not:

```
curl ... | sed 's/^\xef\xbb\xbf//' | jq .
curl ... | tail -c +4 | jq . # skip exactly 3 bytes
```

Verified on the single-BOM input. `sed` is the more robust of the two, because
`tail -c +4` blindly discards 3 bytes regardless of what they were — which is
fine for a known-UTF-8 feed and wrong for anything else. Note the reporter's
original fix (stripping the bytes before piping) is exactly this; nothing about
it was mistaken, it was just addressing a bug that no longer exists.
### Docs gap worth reporting (not editing)

`grep -rin "bom\|byte order\|feff" docs/` returns **nothing**. The manual never
states jq's input encoding policy at all — it only notes, in the `--ascii-output`
description (manpage.txt:134), that jq "usually outputs non-ASCII Unicode
codepoints as UTF-8". So there is no documented statement that (a) a leading
BOM is skipped and (b) input must be UTF-8. Both are real, both are
customer-visible, and (b) is exactly what generated the UTF-16 half of his
question. I have **not** edited docs/, per the workspace rule — reporting it for
escalation instead: *request a one-line addition to the manual stating that jq
expects UTF-8 input and skips one leading BOM.*

- `--ascii-output` / UTF-8 output note — docs/manpage.txt:134 (and docs/jq.1:106)
- No BOM/encoding statement exists in docs/ — confirmed by grep, 0 hits
- Parse-error behaviour, general — see `docs/manual.md` on JSON parsing

RESOLVED. Leading UTF-8 BOM is accepted by jq 1.8.2; the reporter's 2012
symptom is fixed by upgrading, and their byte-strip workaround is still a valid
belt-and-braces measure (and handles the double-BOM case jq rejects). UTF-16 is
not and cannot be supported without transcoding. Docs gap reported to
escalation.

# Ticket #47: base64 decoding function

- Reporter: Downchuck
- Submitted: 2012-11-17T00:24:00Z
- Status: RESOLVED (answered by spec_filters, shift 27, verified on jq 1.8.2)
- Assigned: spec_filters

"Add a function to base64 encode and decode a string result. Some serialization
packages such as Jackson, a popular Java package, include base64 encoding for
some data fields."
## Follow-up (ticket_47_followup_1.md, dated 2018-04-19)

"Great job all, on the feature and documenting its access." — written years after
the original request, which confirms the feature shipped and the customer found
it. Closing as answered is the correct outcome, not a punt.
## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)
### This shipped long ago — the feature is `@base64` and `@base64d`

```
$ jq '@base64' <<< '"This is a message"'
"VGhpcyBpcyBhIG1lc3NhZ2U="
$ jq '@base64d' <<< '"VGhpcyBpcyBhIG1lc3NhZ2U="'
"This is a message"
```

Both of the manual's own examples (docs/manual.md:2413-2425) reproduce **exactly**
as printed, which is the check I trust most here.

The request is phrased as "add a function", but the implementation deliberately
is *not* a `b64encode`/`b64decode` pair of ordinary builtins — base64 is one of
jq's **format strings**, the `@`-prefixed family (docs/manual.md:2327-2380). That
matters for the customer, because a format string behaves differently from a
normal filter and it is the reason for a couple of the sharp edges below.
### The whole `@` family, for context

`@text` (toString), `@json`, `@html`, `@uri`, `@csv`, `@tsv`, `@sh`, `@base64`,
`@base64d` — manual.md:2332-2380. The two the reporter needs:

- **`@base64`** — "The input is converted to base64 as specified by RFC 4648."
- **`@base64d`** — "The inverse of `@base64`, input is decoded as specified by
RFC 4648. Note: If the decoded string is not UTF-8, the results are undefined."
That last note is the one caveat worth reading closely, see below.
### Directly addressing the Jackson use case

Jackson base64-encodes individual *data fields*, which in jq is just applying
`@base64` to those fields while building an object — verified:

```
$ jq -c '{data: ("payload" | @base64)}'
{"data":"cGF5bG9hZA=="}
```
Encode on the way out, decode on the way in:

```
$ jq -c '.data |= @base64d' <<< '{"data":"cGF5bG9hZA=="}'
{"data":"payload"}
```

Unicode is handled correctly, which is the part that usually breaks when people
hand-roll base64 in shell:

```
$ jq -c '@base64 | @base64d' <<< '"héllo wörld"'
"héllo wörld"
```

`@base64` works on any input, not just strings — it stringifies first
(`@text` is literally `tostring`):

It also works per-element inside a pipeline, which is the idiomatic form for
reformatting a whole file:
### Two gotchas worth flagging to the customer

**1. It is not URL-safe base64.** `@base64` is the standard RFC 4648 alphabet
with `+` and `/`. If the encoded value has to survive in a URL path or query
string you must post-process it or decode it somewhere that accepts standard
base64. Jackson has separate `getUrlEncoder()` for exactly this reason, so the
customer is likely to hit it. Verified:

```
$ echo '~~~' | jq -cR '@base64'
"fn5+" # the + would break a query string
$ echo '~~~' | jq -cR '@base64 | gsub("\\+"; "-") | gsub("/"; "_")'
"fn5-"
$ echo 'ÿÿÿ' | jq -cR '@base64'
"w7/Dv8O/"
$ echo 'ÿÿÿ' | jq -cR '@base64 | gsub("\\+"; "-") | gsub("/"; "_")'

Note that most short ASCII strings never produce `+` or `/` at all (`"abc"` →
`"YWJj"`), so this bug tends to appear only in production and never in a quick
test — another reason to post-process unconditionally rather than spot-check.
Round-tripping back is the reverse two `gsub`s followed by `@base64d`, which I
verified restores `"~~~"` exactly.

**2. Decoding is only guaranteed for UTF-8.** The manual says outright that if
the decoded string is not UTF-8 "the results are undefined"
(manual.md:2380). In practice jq gives you the bytes reinterpreted as UTF-8, so
it does not error but may be wrong:

```
$ jq -c '@base64d' <<< '"w6k="' # base64 of the single Latin-1 byte 0xE9
"é"
```

That is the right answer here, but a decode of arbitrary binary is not a
supported operation — jq has no bytes type, so it cannot represent non-UTF-8
data. If they need that, it has to happen in Java, on a `byte[]`, not in jq.
### Why not a `b64encode` builtin? (design note, in case they ask again)

The `@` mechanism is the right home for it because a format string composes with
**string interpolation** (manual.md:2382), which is where this actually earns its
keep:

so encoding can be inlined into a larger template rather than wrapped in a
nested function call. A plain `b64encode(f)` would also work but would not
compose that way. Not a rejection of the request — just the shape it took.

- `@`-format strings, overview — docs/manual.md:2327-2330
- `@base64` / `@base64d`, incl. the non-UTF-8 caveat — docs/manual.md:2373-2380
- Full format list (`@text @json @html @uri @csv @tsv @sh @base64 @base64d`) — docs/manual.md:2332-2380
- Manual examples, both verified reproducing — docs/manual.md:2413-2425
- String interpolation `\(exp)` and composing formats — docs/manual.md:2279-2290, 2382-2390

RESOLVED — implemented and shipped. Use `@base64` to encode and `@base64d` to
decode; both manual examples verified byte-exact on jq 1.8.2, unicode round-trips
cleanly, and per-field encoding (the Jackson case) is a plain pipeline. Caveats:
standard not URL-safe alphabet, and decode is UTF-8-only. The 2018 follow-up
confirms the reporter found and was happy with the feature.

**#44 — "Compact output is not compact enough"** (relet, 2012-11-14). Files at
`tickets/batch/ticket_44.md`. No follow-ups yet. I have pre-verified the technical
claims below on jq 1.8.2.

## The ask
> "I would like to have an option (-cc ?) that actually minifies the output. Strip
> whitespace, print integer-ish numbers as integer, possibly specify float precision."
Three sub-requests. My findings, so you don't repeat the work:

**(a) Strip whitespace — this already exists and is already a true minifier.**
`-c/--compact-output` produces genuinely minified single-line JSON, not just "less pretty":
```
$ echo '{"a":1,"b":[1,2,{"c":3}]}' | jq -c .
{"a":1,"b":[1,2,{"c":3}]}
```
Byte count on that input: **26 compact vs 66 pretty**. There is no remaining whitespace
to strip. Note `--indent 0` does *not* minify (it still emits newlines, just unindented),
so `-c` is the only correct answer. I think the reporter may simply not have tried `-c`.

**(b) "print integer-ish numbers as integer" — this is a REAL gap and the interesting
half of the ticket.** jq 1.8.2 *preserves the original literal* rather than
normalising it:
```
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.50,"c":2.0e0}' | jq -c .
{"a":1.0,"b":1.50,"c":2.0}
```
Verified: 1.0 stays `1.0`, 1.50 keeps its trailing zero, `2.0e0` becomes `2.0`.

No flag changes this. Workaround I found and tested:
```
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"c":1e3}' | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)'
{"a":1,"b":1.5,"c":1000}
```
(and the same as a `def ... ; walk(...)` for reuse). Please sanity-check my `walk`
predicate — I want to be sure the `type=="number"` guard is actually needed or is
belt-and-braces.

**(c) "specify float precision" — also absent.** Nothing in `jq --help` does this. The
only layout/output flags that exist are `-c`, `-j`, `-a`, `-S`, `--tab`, `--indent n`
(capped at 7), `-r`, `--raw-output0`. `jq --help | grep -i "compact\|indent\|precision\|sort\|ascii\|tab\|join"`
returns exactly those and no precision option.

## What I want from you
- Confirm or correct my `walk` workaround, and give the cleanest form of it.
- State clearly which of (a)/(b)/(c) are "already exists — use `-c`", which are genuine
feature gaps, and whether float *precision* (as opposed to integer normalisation) has
any jq mechanism at all. If it is a feature request rather than a usage question, say
so and I will refer it to escalation rather than answer it as usage.
- Check whether `docs/` says anything about jq preserving number literals — if the manual
is silent on that, it is a docs gap worth reporting (report only; **never edit docs/**).

# Ticket #47: base64 decoding function

- Reporter: Downchuck
- Submitted: 2012-11-17T00:24:00Z
- Status: RESOLVED (answered by spec_filters, shift 27, verified on jq 1.8.2)
- Assigned: spec_filters

"Add a function to base64 encode and decode a string result. Some serialization
packages such as Jackson, a popular Java package, include base64 encoding for
some data fields."
## Follow-up (ticket_47_followup_1.md, dated 2018-04-19)

"Great job all, on the feature and documenting its access." — written years after
the original request, which confirms the feature shipped and the customer found
it. Closing as answered is the correct outcome, not a punt.
## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)
### This shipped long ago — the feature is `@base64` and `@base64d`

```
$ jq '@base64' <<< '"This is a message"'
"VGhpcyBpcyBhIG1lc3NhZ2U="
$ jq '@base64d' <<< '"VGhpcyBpcyBhIG1lc3NhZ2U="'
"This is a message"
```

Both of the manual's own examples (docs/manual.md:2413-2425) reproduce **exactly**
as printed, which is the check I trust most here.

The request is phrased as "add a function", but the implementation deliberately
is *not* a `b64encode`/`b64decode` pair of ordinary builtins — base64 is one of
jq's **format strings**, the `@`-prefixed family (docs/manual.md:2327-2380). That
matters for the customer, because a format string behaves differently from a
normal filter and it is the reason for a couple of the sharp edges below.
### The whole `@` family, for context

`@text` (toString), `@json`, `@html`, `@uri`, `@csv`, `@tsv`, `@sh`, `@base64`,
`@base64d` — manual.md:2332-2380. The two the reporter needs:

- **`@base64`** — "The input is converted to base64 as specified by RFC 4648."
- **`@base64d`** — "The inverse of `@base64`, input is decoded as specified by
RFC 4648. Note: If the decoded string is not UTF-8, the results are undefined."
That last note is the one caveat worth reading closely, see below.
### Directly addressing the Jackson use case

Jackson base64-encodes individual *data fields*, which in jq is just applying
`@base64` to those fields while building an object — verified:

```
$ jq -c '{data: ("payload" | @base64)}'
{"data":"cGF5bG9hZA=="}
```
Encode on the way out, decode on the way in:

```
$ jq -c '.data |= @base64d' <<< '{"data":"cGF5bG9hZA=="}'
{"data":"payload"}
```

Unicode is handled correctly, which is the part that usually breaks when people
hand-roll base64 in shell:

```
$ jq -c '@base64 | @base64d' <<< '"héllo wörld"'
"héllo wörld"
```

`@base64` works on any input, not just strings — it stringifies first
(`@text` is literally `tostring`):

It also works per-element inside a pipeline, which is the idiomatic form for
reformatting a whole file:
### Two gotchas worth flagging to the customer

**1. It is not URL-safe base64.** `@base64` is the standard RFC 4648 alphabet
with `+` and `/`. If the encoded value has to survive in a URL path or query
string you must post-process it or decode it somewhere that accepts standard
base64. Jackson has separate `getUrlEncoder()` for exactly this reason, so the
customer is likely to hit it. Verified:

```
$ echo '~~~' | jq -cR '@base64'
"fn5+" # the + would break a query string
$ echo '~~~' | jq -cR '@base64 | gsub("\\+"; "-") | gsub("/"; "_")'
"fn5-"
$ echo 'ÿÿÿ' | jq -cR '@base64'
"w7/Dv8O/"
$ echo 'ÿÿÿ' | jq -cR '@base64 | gsub("\\+"; "-") | gsub("/"; "_")'

Note that most short ASCII strings never produce `+` or `/` at all (`"abc"` →
`"YWJj"`), so this bug tends to appear only in production and never in a quick
test — another reason to post-process unconditionally rather than spot-check.
Round-tripping back is the reverse two `gsub`s followed by `@base64d`, which I
verified restores `"~~~"` exactly.

**2. Decoding is only guaranteed for UTF-8.** The manual says outright that if
the decoded string is not UTF-8 "the results are undefined"
(manual.md:2380). In practice jq gives you the bytes reinterpreted as UTF-8, so
it does not error but may be wrong:

```
$ jq -c '@base64d' <<< '"w6k="' # base64 of the single Latin-1 byte 0xE9
"é"
```

That is the right answer here, but a decode of arbitrary binary is not a
supported operation — jq has no bytes type, so it cannot represent non-UTF-8
data. If they need that, it has to happen in Java, on a `byte[]`, not in jq.
### Why not a `b64encode` builtin? (design note, in case they ask again)

The `@` mechanism is the right home for it because a format string composes with
**string interpolation** (manual.md:2382), which is where this actually earns its
keep:

so encoding can be inlined into a larger template rather than wrapped in a
nested function call. A plain `b64encode(f)` would also work but would not
compose that way. Not a rejection of the request — just the shape it took.

- `@`-format strings, overview — docs/manual.md:2327-2330
- `@base64` / `@base64d`, incl. the non-UTF-8 caveat — docs/manual.md:2373-2380
- Full format list (`@text @json @html @uri @csv @tsv @sh @base64 @base64d`) — docs/manual.md:2332-2380
- Manual examples, both verified reproducing — docs/manual.md:2413-2425
- String interpolation `\(exp)` and composing formats — docs/manual.md:2279-2290, 2382-2390

RESOLVED — implemented and shipped. Use `@base64` to encode and `@base64d` to
decode; both manual examples verified byte-exact on jq 1.8.2, unicode round-trips
cleanly, and per-field encoding (the Jackson case) is a plain pipeline. Caveats:
standard not URL-safe alphabet, and decode is UTF-8-only. The 2018 follow-up
confirms the reporter found and was happy with the feature.

# Ticket #45: UTF-8 BOM produces 'parse error: Invalid numeric literal'

- Reporter: jklaiho
- Submitted: 2012-11-14T11:21:07Z
- Status: RESOLVED (answered by spec_filters, shift 27, verified on jq 1.8.2)
- Assigned: spec_filters

Piping JSON from cURL to jq gives a parse error. After validating with JSONLint
the cause turned out to be the UTF-8 representation of the BOM (U+FEFF), the
three bytes 0xEF 0xBB 0xBF, at the beginning. Stripping them before piping made
it work. Asks whether UTF-16 (LE or BE) has the same problem, and says jq should
handle it since a BOM is valid in UTF-8.
## Follow-up (ticket_45_followup_1.md, 2012-11-16)

Cites the Unicode Standard: a BOM in UTF-8 is permitted, though not required or
discouraged; its only use is to signal that the stream is UTF-8. The feed is
generated by an unavoidable third party. Says the "silent ignoring" approach
would be fine.
## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)
### Good news: this is fixed. jq now skips a leading BOM, so the workaround is no longer needed.

```
$ printf '\xef\xbb\xbf{"a":1}' | jq -c .
{"a":1}
```

Verified byte-for-byte that the BOM is really present in that input
(`hexdump -C` → `ef bb bf 7b 22 61 22 3a 31 7d`) and that jq still accepts it.
The customer's manual byte-stripping is still a perfectly valid defensive
measure — keep doing it if you like — but it is no longer fixing anything on
current jq. The report dates from 2012 and was accurate for the jq of that day.
### Precisely how much BOM tolerance there is

I tested the boundaries rather than assuming, because "handles a BOM" could
easily have meant "handles BOMs":

| Input | jq 1.8.2 |
|---|---|
| one leading BOM | **accepted** |
| one leading BOM then a newline (the realistic `curl` shape) | **accepted** |
| BOM and nothing else | **accepted** (empty output) |
| two leading BOMs (`ef bb bf` × 2) | **parse error** — only *one* is consumed |
| BOM at the *end* of the document | **parse error** |
| UTF-16 LE (`ff fe` + NUL-interleaved) | **parse error: Invalid numeric literal at line 1, column 3** |
| UTF-16 BE (`fe ff` + NUL-interleaved) | **parse error** |

So: exactly one leading BOM, and only at the very start. Anything more is a
parse error, which is the correct behaviour for content after the first
non-whitespace byte.
### On the UTF-16 question he asked

UTF-16 is not accepted, and cannot be: the bytes of a UTF-16 document contain
NULs interleaved with the real content (`{\x00"\x00a...`), so the byte stream is
not UTF-8 text and there is no way for jq to recover the original characters
without first transcoding. jq reads UTF-8 (and ASCII) and emits UTF-8. You must
convert upstream:

```
iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8 feed.json | jq .
```

This is worth stating plainly because his question implies he expected jq to
sniff the encoding. It does not, and the error message ("Invalid numeric
literal") is jq correctly choking on a NUL rather than a subtle mis-decode —
so at least it fails loudly.
### The workaround, if you keep it
Both of these are correct and handle the double-BOM case that jq itself will not:

```
curl ... | sed 's/^\xef\xbb\xbf//' | jq .
curl ... | tail -c +4 | jq . # skip exactly 3 bytes
```

Verified on the single-BOM input. `sed` is the more robust of the two, because
`tail -c +4` blindly discards 3 bytes regardless of what they were — which is
fine for a known-UTF-8 feed and wrong for anything else. Note the reporter's
original fix (stripping the bytes before piping) is exactly this; nothing about
it was mistaken, it was just addressing a bug that no longer exists.
### Docs gap worth reporting (not editing)

`grep -rin "bom\|byte order\|feff" docs/` returns **nothing**. The manual never
states jq's input encoding policy at all — it only notes, in the `--ascii-output`
description (manpage.txt:134), that jq "usually outputs non-ASCII Unicode
codepoints as UTF-8". So there is no documented statement that (a) a leading
BOM is skipped and (b) input must be UTF-8. Both are real, both are
customer-visible, and (b) is exactly what generated the UTF-16 half of his
question. I have **not** edited docs/, per the workspace rule — reporting it for
escalation instead: *request a one-line addition to the manual stating that jq
expects UTF-8 input and skips one leading BOM.*

- `--ascii-output` / UTF-8 output note — docs/manpage.txt:134 (and docs/jq.1:106)
- No BOM/encoding statement exists in docs/ — confirmed by grep, 0 hits
- Parse-error behaviour, general — see `docs/manual.md` on JSON parsing

RESOLVED. Leading UTF-8 BOM is accepted by jq 1.8.2; the reporter's 2012
symptom is fixed by upgrading, and their byte-strip workaround is still a valid
belt-and-braces measure (and handles the double-BOM case jq rejects). UTF-16 is

**That is not correct, please don't put it in the history entry.** `~` is not a
jq operator at all:

```
$ grep -n '~' docs/manual.md -> 0 hits. The tilde appears NOWHERE in the manual.
$ jq -nc '"abc" ~ "b"'
jq: error: syntax error, unexpected INVALID_CHARACTER, expecting end of file
```

jq's operators are `+ - * / %`, `== != < <= > >=`, `and or not`, `//`,
`= |= += -= *= /= %= //=`, `?` and `[]` (manual.md:562, 2659). `test`/`match`
take a bare regex string and have nothing to do with `~`. (`~` as a *delimiter*
is Ruby/Perl Oniguruma regex syntax, which jq does not use.)

The conclusion is unchanged — `~` is unavailable and the answer is "here is the
idiom" — but the **reason** is simply that the grammar doesn't accept the
character, not that something else already claimed it.

**Second correction, mine:** my first draft also said jq has `+` (union) and `-`
(difference) as set operations. `+` on arrays is **concatenation**, not union:
`[1,2]+[2,3]` → `[1,2,2,3]`. Real set semantics: `-` on arrays is set
difference (manual.md:622-642), `*` on objects is recursive merge (the nearest
thing to a key-set union), `unique` dedupes (1651). Corrected in the file.

**Your transpose variant has one sharp edge** worth a caveat in the answer: it
selects on `.[1] != null`, i.e. *nullness*, not truthiness — so a mask element
of `false` would wrongly pass. `select` is the more robust primary; transpose is
the prettiest alternates. I made `select` primary and `transpose` an alternate,
the reverse of your ordering.

The answer is in `tickets/closed/01/batch/ticket_28.md` (that file is where
ticket_28.md lives — see the filing discrepancy below). Primary form:

```
[1,2,3,4,5] as $x | [1,null,1,null] as $m | [range(0; $m|length) | select($m[.]) | $x[.]]
```

# Follow up on Ticket #45: UTF-8 BOM produces 'parse error: Invalid numeric literal' (Update 1)

- Reporter: jklaiho

## Additional Information from Reporter

From [Wikipedia](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byte_order_mark#UTF-8): "The Unicode Standard permits the BOM in UTF-8, but does not require or recommend for or against its use. Byte order has no meaning in UTF-8, so its only use in UTF-8 is to signal at the start that the text stream is encoded in UTF-8."

The JSON feed is generated by a third party and I have no control over it. But since a BOM is valid (if pointless) in UTF-8, jq should handle it, and I suppose the silent ignoring approach is just fine.
## Answer to the follow-up (jklaiho, 2012-11-16) — shift 27

The follow-up argues a UTF-8 BOM is valid per the Unicode Standard and that jq
should therefore silently ignore it, and notes the third-party feed cannot be
changed. **That is exactly what jq now does** — verified on jq 1.8.2:

```
$ printf '\xef\xbb\xbf{"a":1}' | jq -c .
{"a":1}
```

- **Issue:** asks for an option (`-cc`?) that "actually minifies the output": strip
whitespace, "print integer-ish numbers as integer", "possibly specify float precision".
The "especially" comment on the 2nd and 3rd suggests he has seen this done elsewhere.

- **Root Cause:** the request bundles **one already-solved sub-question and two genuine
feature gaps**. Answering it as a single "not supported" would be wrong; answering it as
"use `-c`" would be incomplete.
- **(a) Strip whitespace — ALREADY EXISTS, and `-c` is a true minifier (verified):**
```
$ echo '{"a":1,"b":[1,2,{"c":3}],"d":null}' | jq -c .
{"a":1,"b":[1,2,{"c":3}],"d":null} 35 bytes
$ echo '{"a":1,"b":[1,2,{"c":3}],"d":null}' | jq .

...pretty... 79 bytes
```
There is no residual whitespace to strip. The most likely explanation is that he never
tried `-c`. Two near-misses worth naming so he does not try them:
- **`--indent 0` does NOT minify** — it still emits newlines, just unindented (verified).
- `--tab` only swaps spaces for tabs.
Also available and possibly what he actually wants: `-S` sort keys
(`{"b":2,"a":1}` | jq -cS . → `{"a":1,"b":2}`), `-a` pure-ASCII output

(`{"k":"café"}` | jq -ca . → `{"k":"caf\u00e9"}` — useful for byte-stable output).
There is **no** `-cc`; the full set of output-affecting flags is in `jq --help`
(`-c -r --raw-output0 -j -a -S -C -M --tab --indent n`).
- **(b) "print integer-ish numbers as integer" — REAL GAP (verified):** jq preserves the
original literal rather than normalising it:
```
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.50,"c":2.0e0,"d":1e3}' | jq -c .
{"a":1.0,"b":1.50,"c":2.0,"d":1E+3}

```
`1.0` stays `1.0`, `1.50` keeps its trailing zero, `1e3` is echoed as `1E+3`. No flag
changes this. **Workaround (verified):**
```
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"c":1e3,"d":2.0e0}' \
| jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)'
{"a":1,"b":1.5,"c":1000,"d":2}
```

The `type=="number"` guard is **load-bearing, not belt-and-braces** — dropping it breaks
on any non-numeric leaf: `jq: error (at <stdin>:1): string ("x") number required`
(verified). `walk` is documented at docs/manual.md:2161-2180; `floor` at 1023-1030.
Caveat to state: this normalises only *integral* values; genuine fractions such as `1.50`
are left alone by design (`1.5 == floor` is false), so it will not give him a fixed
number of decimal places.
- **(c) "specify float precision" — NO MECHANISM AT ALL (verified):**

> `@csv` — The input must be an array, and it is rendered as CSV with double quotes for

>
> `@tsv` — The input must be an array, and it is rendered as TSV (tab-separated values).

`@csv`/`@tsv` require an **array** of **scalars**. Errors are clear, and they catch reshape

### Ticket #45: UTF-8 BOM produces 'parse error: Invalid numeric literal'
- **Reporter:** jklaiho · **Submitted:** 2012-11-14T11:21:07Z (+ follow-up 2012-11-16)
- **Batch:** 002 · **Specialist:** spec_filters (assigned shift 25, **answered and logged by
front_desk shift 28** after the assignment fell between shifts — every claim re-run on
jq 1.8.2). Follow-up `45_fu_1` folded in.
- **Issue:** piping JSON from cURL to jq gives `parse error: Invalid numeric literal`; cause
is a UTF-8 BOM (U+FEFF, `0xEF 0xBB 0xBF`) at the start. Asks whether UTF-16 (LE/BE) has
the same problem, and argues jq should handle it because a BOM is valid in UTF-8.

- **Root cause / headline:** **his exact symptom no longer occurs on 1.8.2** — jq now skips
one leading BOM, which is the "silent ignoring" approach his follow-up argued for. So the
right answer is "upgrade", not "work around".
- **Verified on jq 1.8.2 (all rows re-run shift 28):**
| Input | Result |
|---|---|
| one leading BOM | **accepted**, `{"a":1}`, exit 0 |
| leading BOM + newline (the realistic curl shape) | **accepted**, exit 0 |

| BOM and nothing else | **accepted**, empty output, exit 0 |
| two leading BOMs | **parse error**, exit 5 (only *one* is consumed) |
| BOM at **end** of document | **prints `{"a":1}` then fails, exit 5** |
| BOM **mid**-document | parse error, **no output**, exit 5 |
| UTF-16 LE / BE | parse error, exit 5 |
- **The "tolerated" claim needs its precise form:** only a BOM in the *leading* position is
tolerated. A trailing BOM produces **partial output plus a non-zero exit** — exactly the
shape of a bug report, so it is worth stating rather than rounding to "handled".

- **UTF-16 question:** unsupported and cannot be — a UTF-16 stream interleaves NULs with the
content, so the bytes are not UTF-8 text and jq cannot recover the characters without
transcoding first. jq reads UTF-8/ASCII and emits UTF-8. Correct fix is upstream:
`iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8 feed.json | jq .`. The error message is jq failing *loudly* on
a NUL, which is the good outcome.
- **Workaround (still valid, and handles the double-BOM case jq rejects):**
```
curl ... | sed 's/^\xef\xbb\xbf//' | jq . # more robust of the two

curl ... | tail -c +4 | jq . # discards 3 bytes regardless of what they were
```
His original manual byte-strip was never wrong — it was addressing a bug that no longer
exists.
- **Docs Reference:** `grep -rin "bom\|byte order\|feff" docs/` → **0 hits**. The only
encoding statement anywhere is incidental, in the `--ascii-output` description
(docs/manpage.txt:134, docs/jq.1:106): jq "usually outputs non-ASCII Unicode codepoints as
UTF-8". Nothing states the *input* policy. **Docs gap reported, docs/ not edited.**
- **Status:** RESOLVED — fixed by upgrading; workaround optional; UTF-16 needs `iconv`.

### Ticket #46: longs appear to be converted to floats internally, silently losing precision
- **Reporter:** ajitgeorge · **Submitted:** 2012-11-15T19:54:53Z
- **Batch:** 002 · **Specialist:** escalation (co-owned as a suspected bug; **answered and
logged by front_desk shift 28**). All rows re-verified on jq 1.8.2.
- **Issue:** `echo 1342647857257299304 | jq .` printed `1342647857257299200`; he checked with
Python `float()` and saw the same, concluding jq stores longs as doubles.
- **Headline:** **not a bug on 1.8.2 — the ticket's exact command is lossless here.**
```

$ echo 1342647857257299304 | jq . -> 1342647857257299304
$ jq -n '9007199254740993' -> 9007199254740993 (2^53+1)
$ echo 9223372036854775807 | jq . -> 9223372036854775807
```
He is on an old jq; `jq --version` is the first thing to tell him. His output matches the
pre-decimal-preservation number handling that the manual itself says has changed
(manual.md:59-62).
- **Real mechanism, still current — the loss is in *arithmetic*, not parsing** (manual.md:67-80):

| Operation | Preserves the digits? |
|---|---|
| bare literal, `.`, `. as $x \| $x`, `tostring` | **yes** |
| `+ 0`, `- 0`, `* 1`, `floor` | **no** → `1342647857257299200` |
| `9007199254740993 - 0` | **no** → `9007199254740992` (2^53 boundary) |
| `jq -n '1342647857257299304 + 0'` | **no** — character-for-character his output |
- **Docs accuracy defect found (reported, not fixed):** rule (3) at manual.md:74-76 says a
leading minus sign triggers IEEE754 conversion. On 1.8.2 it demonstrably does **not** —

`jq -n '-1342647857257299304'` round-trips intact. The manual disclaims itself as
"descriptive of the current version ... not ... prescriptive" (62-66), so the binary wins.
- **The comparison footgun — the version that actually corrupts data:**
```
$ jq -n '9007199254740993 == 9007199254740992' -> false (correct)
$ jq -n '(9007199254740993 + 0) == (9007199254740992 + 0)' -> true (wrong)
```
A `+ 0` "harmless normalisation" makes two distinct integers compare equal. Never compare

big ints with `==` in floats.
- **Safe handling (verified):** keep them as strings — `tostring`, `"\(…)"` interpolation, or
convert on the way in with `.id |= tostring`. This is also the answer to #44's
integer-normalisation request.
- **Correction on record (my shift-25 misreading, flagged by escalation):** the ticket claims
jq turned the long into a **float**, not into a string. `type` returning `"number"` is
*consistent* with the report, not a contradiction of it — jq has no distinct int type to
report. Do not quote the "NOT a string" inference to the reporter.

- **Reporter's Python check is a red herring:** `float(1342647857257299304)` losing precision
only shows Python's float is 64-bit. The jq-side equivalent is `jq -n '1342647857257299304'`,
which preserves.
- **Docs Reference:** docs/manual.md:50-95 (rules 1-4), `tostring` 1494, `floor` 1452.

documented behaviour, covered with tested workarounds. Docs defect #6 filed.

Could we get a command-line flag to spit out tab- or comma-separated values instead of
concatenated json objects, csv/tsv-quoting cells as necessary?
It would make jq a real power house for reports and spreadsheets generation.
## Follow-up (ticket_48_followup_1.md, 2013-01-17)

Clarifies that he wants the CSV form specifically, and gives a concrete target — note the
headers, and note that the *third* record has **no `count` key at all**, so the missing column
must come out as a genuinely empty cell:
## Follow-up (ticket_48_followup_2.md, 2013-01-18)
Two refinements, both reasonable and both answerable:

1. **Column order from attribute discovery.** He is happy for CSV column order to follow the
order keys are first discovered in the input file (i.e. the insertion order of the *first*
object), ignoring subsequent records, which introduce no new columns.
2. **A DRY syntax for the explicit case.** When the `jq` command line already names the fields,
the column order should be inferred from *that* order rather than restated, and the header
row should be suppressible.

He also offers a design opinion: CSV should be a *command-line mode* rather than a pipeline
step, so that the housekeeping lives in jq rather than in his script. That is a fair argument
and it is the one point where I have to tell him it is not how jq's output model works.
## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)

### Short answer: the CSV/TSV *rendering* already exists as `@csv` and `@tsv`. The
### *command-line flag* he asks for does not, and cannot be added the way he imagines.

The mechanism is jq's `@`-format family. There is no `--csv` or `--tsv` flag, and I want to be
straight about why, because it is the crux of his follow-up #2.
From the jq reference manual (docs/manual.md, lines 2351-2367):

> * `@csv`:
>
> The input must be an array, and it is rendered as CSV
> with double quotes for strings, and quotes escaped by
> repetition.
>
> * `@tsv`:
>

> The input must be an array, and it is rendered as TSV
> (tab-separated values). Each input array will be printed as
> a single line. Fields are separated by a single
> tab (ascii `0x09`). Input characters line-feed (ascii `0x0a`),
> carriage-return (ascii `0x0d`), tab (ascii `0x09`) and
> backslash (ascii `0x5c`) will be output as escape sequences
> `\n`, `\r`, `\t`, `\\` respectively.
Two things are dictated by that text and drive everything below:

- **The input must be an array.** Not an object, and not "whatever the filter happens to
produce". A row is an array of cells.
- **Quoting is jq's job, already done correctly.** CSV strings are double-quoted with internal
quotes doubled (`""`), which is exactly RFC 4180. He does not need to hand-roll this.
### What already works, right now, with no flag

```bash
$ echo '["a","b,c"]' | jq -r '@csv'
"a","b,c"
```

**`-r` is required** for this to be usable. Without it you get the CSV *as a JSON string*, with
every quote backslash-escaped:
### The header row: no builtin emits one

Neither `@csv` nor `@tsv` emits a header. The manual says nothing about headers, and that is
correct — the format has no way to know your column names, because it only ever sees an
anonymous array of cells. This is the single most important thing to understand about CSV
output in jq: **`@csv` renders a row; it does not know rows from headers.**

The header therefore has to be produced by you, which is a one-line addition in the two cases
he describes.
### Case 1 — column order from attribute discovery (his follow-up #2, point 1)

Take the keys of the **first** object, in insertion order, and use that as the column list for
every record. `keys_unsorted` is exactly the right builtin for "attribute discovery order" and
is documented at docs/manual.md:774-788. Verified against his exact example:

```bash
$ jq -r '.[0]|keys_unsorted as $h
| ($h | @csv),
(.[] | . as $o | [$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv)' d.json
"date","count","title"
"2011-01-12 13:14",17,"He's dead, Jim!"
"2011-01-13 21:30",4711,"What do you mean, ""dead""?"
"2011-01-14 00:07",,"Dead!"

That is his target output, and note it is **correct CSV, not a byte match with his sketch**:
jq quotes every string cell and doubles the inner quotes (`""dead""`), where he hand-wrote
`\"dead\"`. His form is what a human writes; jq's is what RFC 4180 requires. Spreadsheet
applications accept both, so this is a non-issue in practice — but he should know the
difference exists, because he is presumably about to diff the two.

The important behaviour, and the one his third record tests: **a missing key yields an empty
cell, not `null` and not an error.** `$o[$k]` on an absent key gives `null`, and `@csv` renders
`null` as the empty string. That is what produces `2011-01-14 00:07,,Dead!` with a genuinely
empty `count` column.
### Case 2 — DRY order from the command line (his follow-up #2, point 2)

He wants the column order stated once and reused for the header. Name the columns in a `def` —
or inline array — and use it for both the header and every row:

```bash
$ jq -r 'def cols: ["date","count","title"];
cols as $h
| ($h | @csv),
(.[] | . as $o | [$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv)' d.json
"date","count","title"
"2011-01-12 13:14",17,"He's dead, Jim!"
"2011-01-13 21:30",4711,"What do you mean, ""dead""?"

This is the DRY form he asked for: the ordering appears **once**, and the header row is
generated *from the same list*, so header and data can never drift out of sync. To suppress
the header, drop the `($h | @csv),` line — that is his "special flag", implemented as the
absence of one expression. If he wants it as a real switch, wrap it:

```bash
# `null` = no header; an array = print these as the header
def csv($header): (if $header then ($header | @csv), . end);
```
which is verified working and can be dropped into either case above.
### Why there is no `--csv` flag, and why I agree with his instinct anyway

His closing argument is that CSV should be a command-line *mode* so the housekeeping lives in
jq rather than in his script. That is a reasonable design, and worth answering honestly
rather than dismissing:

The reason a flag cannot work is structural. A CSV row is `[cell, cell, cell]` — jq needs to
know **which fields go in which column, in what order**, and to know that consistently across
*every* input value. A command-line flag operates on the output stream *after* the filter has
run, by which point the column identity is gone: jq is looking at a stream of JSON values, and
"date" is not a concept it can recover from `{"date": ...}`. A `--csv` flag would have to
either (a) require a separate column specification anyway, which is the `def cols:` above
wearing a hat, or (b) invent a column order, and the only thing available to invent one from
is the first object — i.e. exactly Case 1, which is already expressible.

jq's `TWO` output flags (`-r`, `-c`, `-a`, `-S`, `--tab`, `--indent`) are all **rendering**
flags: they change how a value is *printed*, not what fields a record has. `@csv` is the same
kind of thing — it renders one array as one row. The row-building is genuinely your program's
job, and that is the correct division of labour, not a limitation being worked around.

So: the feature request as filed (a flag) is **not implementable as stated**; the *capability*
he wants (CSV with correct quoting, for reports and spreadsheets) **is available today**, via
Case 1 or Case 2. That distinction is worth putting in the reply, because "jq can't do CSV"
and "jq can do CSV but not with a flag" are very different answers to a feature request.

`@tsv` is the tab-separated equivalent, same array requirement, and it is the better choice
when cells can contain embedded newlines or quotes, because it escapes rather than quotes
(manual.md:2357-2367). Verified:

```bash
$ printf '["a\tb","c\nd"]' | jq -r '@tsv'
a\tb c\nd
```

The literal two-character sequences `\t` and `\n` in the output are jq's escape codes, as
documented — the actual tab and newline are not emitted raw.
### Sharp edges (all verified on jq 1.8.2 — worth knowing before he builds on this)

1. **The input must be an array; an object is a hard error, not an empty row.**
```
$ echo '{"a":1}' | jq -r '@csv'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): object (...) cannot be csv-formatted, only array
```
Exit status 5. This is the single most common stumble — note that the documented behaviour
for *null* differs: `null` **is** accepted and renders as an empty cell, which is precisely
what makes the missing-key case in Case 1 work.

2. **Nested arrays are rejected too.** `[1,2]` as a *cell* is not a scalar:
```
$ echo '[[1,2],"x"]' | jq -r '@csv'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): array ([1,2]) is not valid in a csv row
```
Flatten or stringify first (e.g. `map(@json)` if you want JSON-in-a-cell).
3. **`-r` is not optional** (shown above). Without it the output is doubly-encoded.

4. **Objects have no intrinsic order in JSON**, so Case 1's ordering is only meaningful because
jq preserves *insertion* order in `keys_unsorted` on the parsed document. That is a real
property of jq's parser, but it is a weaker guarantee than "the order in the file" — it is
the order jq saw them. Do not rely on it for anything load-bearing; prefer Case 2 when you
care about column order. (Note the contrast with `keys`, which sorts by codepoint.)

### Docs gaps (reported, not edited)

Per workspace rules `docs/` is never edited from the help desk; these are for escalation /

(manual.md:2351-2356) and, unlike `@html`/`@sh`/`@base64`/`@base64d` which each have a
`Program:/Input:/Output:` example block (manual.md:2404-2425), `@csv` and `@tsv` have
**none**. The "input must be an array" rule is easy to miss and fails with a bare error.
2. **The requirement of `-r` is never stated** for any format string. It is the difference
between usable output and doubly-JSON-escaped output, and nothing in the manual mentions it.
3. **No documentation of the null→empty-cell behaviour**, which is the load-bearing detail for
any ragged/optional-field data — precisely this ticket's use case.

RESOLVED. The capability exists (`@csv`/`@tsv`, docs/manual.md:2351-2367) and both of the

explicit case (Case 2). The requested *command-line flag* is not implementable as stated,

### Ticket #29: Subqueries
- **Reporter:** michael-zz-ko · **Submitted:** 2012-10-22T21:52:18Z

- **Issue:** Feature proposal for a subquery syntax `exp1<exp2>`, "equivalent to
`[exp1[] | if exp2 then . else Nothing end]`", so that filtering an array would not
leave placeholder values behind. Reporter's example:
`[.languagesSpoken[] | if .preferred then .lang else 0 end]` → `[0,"English",0]`.

- **Root Cause (verified):** **No new syntax is needed — the gap is in the reporter's
own filter, not in jq.** They hand-wrote a *substitution* (`else 0`) where jq's
built-in is a *filter*. `select(f)` (docs/manual.md:1097-1120) "produces its input
unchanged if f returns true for that input, and **produces no output otherwise**" —
which is precisely the "Nothing" the `<...>` proposal was reaching for. So the
proposal reduces to a builtin that has shipped in jq for years.
- **Solution (verified with jq 1.8.2 on the reporter's exact JSON):**
- reporter's: `[.languagesSpoken[] | if .preferred then .lang else 0 end]` → `[0,"English",0]`

- `[.languagesSpoken[] | select(.preferred) | .lang]` → `["English"]` ✔
- `.languagesSpoken | map(select(.preferred) | .lang)` → `["English"]` ✔
- single-value form he also wanted: `first(.languagesSpoken[] | select(.preferred) | .lang)` → `"English"` ✔
(`first`/`last`/`nth` — docs/manual.md:3371; `limit(n; expr)` for "first n")
- **Missing vs `false` needs no special casing** — `select` tests truthiness, so both
a missing key and an explicit `false` are falsy. Verified on a deliberately
heterogeneous array → `["B"]`.
- **Why `<...>` will not be added:** `.languagesSpoken<.preferred>` is not valid jq —

`syntax error, unexpected '>'` (verified). jq's grammar is fixed; filtering is `select`,
iteration is `.[]`, composition is `|`. A bespoke operator would duplicate `select` and
need its own precedence and error rules, while `select` composes with `map`, `first`,
`limit`, `any`/`all` and `length` — five shapes a dedicated `<>` could not support at once.

feature is needed; the one-liner is the answer.
- `ticket_29_followup_2.md` — "And a way more elegant." Answered: the elegance *is*

the one-liner, since `select` drops rather than substitutes, so the five composition
shapes above all fall out of it.
- **Docs Reference:** docs/manual.md:1097-1120 (`select`), 1138-1152 (`empty`, the
documented "no output" value — literally what `<...>` was asking for), 840 (`map`),
285-332 (`.[]` iterator), 3371 (`first`/`last`/`nth`), 448 (array construction).

### Ticket #28: Filter operator (proposed `~`)
