## Read this if you use the #44 workaround — the form changed twice

I logged a filter at shift 25 for ticket #44 (normalising `1.0` → `1`). **Both that version
and my first correction were unsafe and corrupted data.** Only this form is correct:

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
```
**How it went wrong, in order:**

1. **Shift 25 (mine, wrong).** `walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)`.
`.==floor` is *true* for exact integers past 2^53, and the `floor` **call** — not the
comparison — forces the IEEE754 conversion (manual.md:66-68):
`{"id":18446744073709551615}` → `{"id":18446744073709552000}`. The `type` guard never
helped here; it only ever excluded strings.
2. **Shift 31 (mine, also wrong).** I added a `(tostring|test("[.eE]"))` gate, which fixed
2^53 but let **`1E+400`** through, and `floor` **saturates** out-of-range doubles to
`1.7976931348623157e+308` — silently, rc=0. I had picked the wrong axis: literal *shape*.

What matters is **magnitude**.
3. **Shift 32 (correct).** spec_builtins found the `1E+400` hole and proposed the magnitude
gate above, which also drops the regex entirely. I re-verified everything independently —
the 16-key torture input, the byte-identical output on the original example, the
saturation behaviour of `floor`/`trunc`/`round`, and the `fabs` short-circuit — and folded
it into history.md as a shift-32 addendum.

**Two caveats that must travel with the filter:**
- `fabs` is *itself* arithmetic and converts too. It is safe here only because `and`
short-circuits before it is evaluated on the big values it would damage, and its result is
never emitted. Anyone lifting `fabs` out of the filter and using it standalone will corrupt
data.
- Do not use `(.-floor) != 0` as a "has a fractional part" test — it truncates real fractions
(`1.5` → `1`).
## The process lesson, which is the part I actually want you to take

**A verified example is not a verified filter.** My verification standard was "does it produce
the output I claimed, on the example I picked" — and the example I picked contained neither a
large integer nor an out-of-range float, so both bugs sailed through my own testing. I gave a
workaround the same trust as a fact I had read in the manual.
The concrete rule I am adopting, and asking you to adopt:

> When verifying a **transformation** (as opposed to a fact lookup), test values *outside* the
> example's range. The high-risk categories are: **IEEE754 / large or out-of-range numbers**,
> **`walk`/`map`/`recurse` over heterogeneous trees**, **string↔number coercion**, and
> **anything with a `type` guard** (the guard constrains one failure mode and can hide another).

Credit where due: spec_transforms caught defect 1 at shift 30 and spec_builtins caught defect
2 at shift 32, both by re-running my own examples with adversarial inputs rather than
re-reading them. That is exactly the right instinct and I would like more of it. Neither
specialist edited `tickets/history.md` — they flagged it and let me fold it in, which is also
the right call.

the output I claimed, on the example I picked" — and the example I picked contained neither a
large integer nor an out-of-range float, so both bugs sailed through my own testing. I gave a
workaround the same trust as a fact I had read in the manual.

inert exactly where it matters.

walk(if type=="number" and (tostring|test("[.eE]")) and .==floor then floor else . end)
```

**plain integers now skip `floor` too**, so a table of small ids is no longer routed
through IEEE754 at all. The gate is doing more work than the old one, not less.

The gate is safe from *corruption*, but it is **not** a general "normalise my numbers"
filter, because `floor` still rewrites the **rendered form** of anything whose literal
contains `.` or an exponent. Verified:

That is **not** data loss — `1e10 == (1e10|floor)` is `true`, and 1e10 is well inside
IEEE754 — but the *lexical* form changes, and if you are diffing files, hashing
canonical output, or round-tripping numbers as text, it will show up as a diff. The
reason is that such literals are small by construction, which is exactly what makes
`floor` harmless to the value and lossy to the text.

integral-looking numbers print as integers"* and the values may be large ids. Do **not**
reach for it when you need byte-stable numeric text. I have not written this into any
ticket or docs — flagging it to you as the team-lead call on whether it becomes a

input instead" is not a workaround for that one.

note as the #44 bug.

**jq cannot evaluate arithmetic as a bare top-level program.** `echo '1 - 0' | jq .`
is a `parse error: Invalid numeric literal`, and so is `3 - 0`. To do arithmetic you
must supply a *filter*, e.g. `echo '1 - 0' | jq '. - 0'` (which yields `-1`). So

worth remembering before we spend time debugging a "jq is broken" report that is

actually a missing filter. (`. - 0` on a big int is also a clean one-call way to
*demonstrate* the #44 corruption.)

# 32_spec_builtins_floor_docs_defect

To: escalation
From: spec_builtins
Shift: 32
Topic: New docs defect — `floor`/`trunc`/`round` are documented without any "not a no-op on integers" warning; plus undocumented saturation on out-of-range doubles
Concrete case attached, found while reviewing the ticket #44 correction.
docs/manual.md:1023-1030 documents `floor` as:
> Round down to the nearest integer.

and `trunc`/`round` alongside it in the same style. Nowhere does it say that **calling one of
these on a value that is already an integer is not a no-op**, and in fact it is not — the call
triggers jq's IEEE754 conversion (docs/manual.md:66-68, "Any arithmetic operation on a number
that has not already been converted to an IEEE754 double precision representation will trigger a
conversion") and silently changes the value.

The trap is that the *guard* people reach for (`if . == floor then floor else . end`) is
**true** for these values, so a natural-looking filter passes them straight into the corrupting
call. The comparison is innocent; the `floor` call is what loses the data.
## 2. Second, sharper defect: saturation on out-of-range doubles

`floor` on a double larger than DBL_MAX does not error — it **saturates** to
1.7976931348623157e+308. Undocumented anywhere:

Exit status 0. The input is silently replaced by a different, merely large-looking, value. I do
not know whether saturation is deliberate (it is consistent with C99 `floor`) or a jq bug, but
either way the manual should say what happens, because a jq program cannot currently predict it.
## 3. Relationship to existing defects

- STATUS.md defect 3 ("manual never says jq preserves number literals") is the *upstream* cause:
preservation is why the unconverted value exists, and the conversion is what destroys it.
- I flagged this at shift 31 as an addendum; this note attaches the two concrete reproducers
and the saturation case, which were not previously recorded with an example.
- Same conversion mechanism already documented under ticket #46 (integer precision loss).
## 4. Suggested docs content (not mine to write — reporting only)

For the `floor`/`trunc`/`round` entries: one sentence that these are arithmetic and therefore
convert the number, so they are **not** safe to apply indiscriminately to integers; note the
out-of-range saturation; and note that a value-safe guard must bound magnitude, e.g.
`if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end`.

I did **not** edit `docs/`. Also not mine: `tickets/history.md`. I have sent the concrete
replacement filter to front_desk to fold into the #44 entry.

# 29_spec_builtins_csv_docs_gaps

To: escalation
From: spec_builtins (shift 29)

Four documentation gaps found while answering ticket #48 (CSV/TSV output) and ticket #45
(BOM/encoding). Per workspace rules I have **not** edited `docs/` — these are for upstream.
## 1. `@csv` and `@tsv` have no worked example

Every other format string has a `Program:/Input:/Output:` block:
`@html`, `@sh`, `@base64`, `@base64d` at **docs/manual.md:2404-2425**. The two tabular formats
have **none** — only three lines of prose each at **docs/manual.md:2351-2367**.

The consequence is that the single most important rule, stated but never demonstrated, fails
opaquely. Feeding an object to `@csv` gives:

```
$ echo '{"a":1}' | jq -r '@csv'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): object (...) cannot be csv-formatted, only array
```

A reader has no way to connect that error to the prose without already understanding that a
row is `[cell, cell, cell]`. A two-line example would fix it.
## 2. The `-r` requirement is documented nowhere

`@foo` applied to a non-`@text`/`@json` format yields a **string**, which jq then prints as a
JSON string unless `-r` is given:

```
$ echo '["a","b"]' | jq '@csv' → "\"a\",\"b\"" (doubly escaped, unusable)
$ echo '["a","b"]' | jq -r '@csv' → "a","b" (correct)
```

This is true of **every** format string, and neither the "Format strings and escaping"
section (manual.md:2327-2400) nor the man page mentions it. A reader following the manual
literally gets output that looks broken. Probably best added as a note to the
`@foo` overview at manual.md:2327-2330, since that is where the syntax is introduced.
## 3. `null` renders as an empty cell in `@csv`/`@tsv` — undocumented

This is the behaviour that makes ragged / optional-field data work at all, and it is the
detail ticket #48 actually turned on:

It is worth stating explicitly, because it is non-obvious and load-bearing: a missing key
resolves to `null`, so `[$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv` yields a correctly empty cell for absent
fields without any special-casing. Note the contrast with a **non-array, non-null** value,
which is a hard error (exit 5):

```
$ echo '[[1,2],"x"]' | jq -r '@csv'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): array ([1,2]) is not valid in a csv row
```
## 4. Input encoding / BOM tolerance is never stated (from ticket #45)

`grep -rin "bom\|byte order\|feff" docs/` → **0 hits** across all three rendered manuals. The
manual does not state jq's input-encoding policy, which produces two behaviours that look like
bugs:

- jq skips **exactly one** leading UTF-8 BOM. A second BOM, or a trailing one, is a parse
error.
- UTF-16 input is impossible (NUL-interleaved bytes are not valid UTF-8); it must be converted
externally, e.g. `iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8`.

Also unstated: that a *non*-UTF-8 BOM in a `@base64d` string decodes to "undefined results"
(that caveat **is** present, at manual.md:2378-2380, but the input-side BOM story is absent).

None of these are correctness bugs in jq itself — all four are documentation omissions. I have
the reproductions for each if you want them turned into an upstream issue. #1-#3 are cheap to
fix (one example block + two sentences) and unblock anyone using jq for reports/spreadsheets.

# 32_front_desk_floor_trap_second_correction

To: all specialists (spec_filters, spec_transforms, spec_builtins, spec_cli_io, escalation)
From: front_desk
Shift: 31 (following notes from spec_transforms sh30 and spec_builtins sh32)
Topic: The #44 `walk(... floor ...)` filter needed a SECOND correction — final form, and the
process lesson I owe the team
## Read this if you use the #44 workaround — the form changed twice

I logged a filter at shift 25 for ticket #44 (normalising `1.0` → `1`). **Both that version
and my first correction were unsafe and corrupted data.** Only this form is correct:

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
```
**How it went wrong, in order:**

1. **Shift 25 (mine, wrong).** `walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)`.
`.==floor` is *true* for exact integers past 2^53, and the `floor` **call** — not the
comparison — forces the IEEE754 conversion (manual.md:66-68):
`{"id":18446744073709551615}` → `{"id":18446744073709552000}`. The `type` guard never
helped here; it only ever excluded strings.
2. **Shift 31 (mine, also wrong).** I added a `(tostring|test("[.eE]"))` gate, which fixed
2^53 but let **`1E+400`** through, and `floor` **saturates** out-of-range doubles to
`1.7976931348623157e+308` — silently, rc=0. I had picked the wrong axis: literal *shape*.

What matters is **magnitude**.
3. **Shift 32 (correct).** spec_builtins found the `1E+400` hole and proposed the magnitude
gate above, which also drops the regex entirely. I re-verified everything independently —
the 16-key torture input, the byte-identical output on the original example, the
saturation behaviour of `floor`/`trunc`/`round`, and the `fabs` short-circuit — and folded
it into history.md as a shift-32 addendum.

**Two caveats that must travel with the filter:**
- `fabs` is *itself* arithmetic and converts too. It is safe here only because `and`
short-circuits before it is evaluated on the big values it would damage, and its result is
never emitted. Anyone lifting `fabs` out of the filter and using it standalone will corrupt
data.
- Do not use `(.-floor) != 0` as a "has a fractional part" test — it truncates real fractions
(`1.5` → `1`).
## The process lesson, which is the part I actually want you to take

**A verified example is not a verified filter.** My verification standard was "does it produce
the output I claimed, on the example I picked" — and the example I picked contained neither a
large integer nor an out-of-range float, so both bugs sailed through my own testing. I gave a
workaround the same trust as a fact I had read in the manual.
The concrete rule I am adopting, and asking you to adopt:

> When verifying a **transformation** (as opposed to a fact lookup), test values *outside* the
> example's range. The high-risk categories are: **IEEE754 / large or out-of-range numbers**,
> **`walk`/`map`/`recurse` over heterogeneous trees**, **string↔number coercion**, and
> **anything with a `type` guard** (the guard constrains one failure mode and can hide another).

Credit where due: spec_transforms caught defect 1 at shift 30 and spec_builtins caught defect
2 at shift 32, both by re-running my own examples with adversarial inputs rather than
re-reading them. That is exactly the right instinct and I would like more of it. Neither
specialist edited `tickets/history.md` — they flagged it and let me fold it in, which is also
the right call.
## Docs defect upgraded (now #7 in board/STATUS.md)

The sharpest version of this is not that the manual omits literal preservation. It is that
**`floor` is documented at manual.md:1023-1030 purely as "Round down to the nearest integer",
with nothing warning that calling it on an already-integral value is not a no-op and can
silently corrupt it** — and its saturation on out-of-range doubles is documented nowhere. A
reader reasonably reads `floor` on an integer as inert; that reasonable reading is the entire
trap. Cross-reference the "any arithmetic operation" wording gap at manual.md:66-68.

For **escalation**: this one is worth considering as an upstream issue, not just a docs fix.
jq demonstrably preserves number literals on bare parse, but `floor` destroys them past 2^53
and saturates past DBL_MAX with no warning and exit 0. The docs and the binary disagree about
whether that is intended behaviour. `docs/` still not edited by anyone.
## Also folded into history.md this shift

- **#45** — spec_cli_io (sh33) independently reproduced the entire BOM boundary table. Added
their trap: a **trailing** BOM emits the valid record on stdout *and* exits 5, so "did I get
my data?" and "did the command succeed?" can disagree. Check exit status, not just non-empty
stdout, in any jq pipeline.
- **#40** — same note added jq's own error text naming the fix (`try .["field"] instead of
.field for unusually named fields`) and a ruling that the `@`-in-keys gap is a **docs gap
first** (new defect #9), since `@context` is mandatory in every JSON-LD document.

it was written after their note was drafted), and the batch is archived at
`tickets/closed/02/`. `tickets/batch/` is empty and awaiting the next announcement.

- **IMPORTANT CORRECTION to front_desk's and my own pre-verification:** front_desk's note (and my first draft) claimed `~` "is the regex match operator, the one behind test/match (manual.md:2874)". **That is wrong.** `~` is *not a jq operator at all*. `grep -n '~' docs/manual.md` → **0 hits**. jq's operators are `+ - * / %`, comparisons, `and or not`, `//`, `= |= += ...`, `?`, `[]`. `"abc" ~ "b"` → `unexpected INVALID_CHARACTER`. Real set ops: `-` on arrays is set difference (manual.md:622-642), `*` on objects is recursive merge (the closest thing to a key-set union), `unique` dedupes (1651).
- **Docs precedent for "boolean mask":** none. `grep -rin "mask\|boolean array" docs/` → 0 hits. Nearest is `paths(f)` (1218-1226) / `getpath` — "give me the positions of the true values" is the same idea, and it *is* documented. So: real idiom, undocumented, no operator needed.
- **Flag:** the `transpose` variant selects on `!= null`, not truthiness, so a mask value of `false` would wrongly pass. `select` is the robust primary.

# Ticket #52: How can I build jq for Windows?

- Reporter: tiendq

> Is there any one can give me a brief instruction to build jq for Windows?
>
> Thanks,
> Tien

For a *brief* instruction: **you almost certainly do not need to build jq.** Prebuilt Windows
binaries are published on the GitHub release page (docs/README.md:12-14), and there is also an
official Docker image (docs/README.md:16-18). Building from source is for people who need a
custom build. If you do need one, the source-build instructions are in `docs/README.md:20-46`
and I reproduce them below with the Windows-specific notes the docs do not cover.
### The documented source build (docs/README.md:20-46)
Dependencies (docs/README.md:22-27): **libtool, make, automake, autoconf**.

```console
git submodule update --init # if building from git, to get oniguruma
autoreconf -i # if building from git
./configure --with-oniguruma=builtin
make -j8
make check
sudo make install
```
Statically linked (docs/README.md:40-44):

```console
make LDFLAGS=-all-static
```

If you are building a **released tarball** rather than git, skip `autoreconf` — and then flex
and bison are not needed either (docs/README.md:46). That is the single most useful line in
the build section, because it is the difference between needing a full autotools + parser
toolchain and needing almost nothing.
### What the docs do NOT tell you about Windows (the real answer to his question)
This is where the documentation is genuinely thin, so here is the substance:

**1. There is no MSVC path, and the docs never say so.** The build system is autotools +
`./configure` + `make`. That is a POSIX toolchain. On Windows you therefore need one of:

- **MSYS2** (recommended — the most complete and current option),
- **Cygwin**,
- the **Windows Subsystem for Linux**, or
- a cross-compilation setup (docs/README.md:48-50 points at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
and the cross-compilation wiki page for this).

The docs do mention MSYS2/Cygwin in one place, but only incidentally and for a different
purpose — jq.1:229 and the equivalent man page text warn that "Windows users using WSL, MSYS2,
or Cygwin, should use this option when using a native jq.exe, otherwise jq will turn newlines
(LFs) into carriage-return-then-newline (CRLF)". That flag is for *running* a native
`jq.exe`, not for building, which is easy to misread.

**2. The MSYS2 route, concretely.** Install MSYS2, then from an MSYS2 shell install the
toolchain and build in the MSYS2 environment (not a plain cmd/PowerShell prompt):

```console
pacman -S --needed base-devel git autoconf automake libtool make bison flex
# then follow docs/README.md:31-38 unchanged
```

Note that jq's own docs list only libtool/make/automake/autoconf as dependencies, but a
**git** build additionally needs `bison` and `flex`, because `autoreconf -i` has to generate
the regex parser. The docs imply this at docs/README.md:46 but never state it as a
dependency. If `autoreconf` fails on a missing `bison.y`/`lexer.l`, that is why.

**3. `--with-oniguruma=builtin` is the flag to care about.** It bundles the Oniguruma regex
engine rather than linking a system copy — important on Windows, where there is no system
Oniguruma to find. jq's own text is explicit that the regex flavour matters:
jq.1:2741 and manpage.txt:2164 both say "jq uses the Oniguruma regular expression library",
and jq.1:2745 notes jq uses the "Perl NG" (Perl with named groups) flavour.

**Worth knowing:** the *reference manual* (docs/manual.md) never mentions Oniguruma at all —
`grep -c oniguruma docs/manual.md` → **0**. It appears only in docs/jq.1 and
docs/manpage.txt. So if you are working purely from the online manual you will not know which
regex engine you are getting, which matters if you plan to port regexes.

**4. How to tell what you actually built.** jq reports its own configuration two ways, and
this is the first thing to ask for when a Windows build misbehaves:

```console
$ jq --build-configuration
--prefix=/usr 'CFLAGS=-march=x86-64 ... -flto=auto' 'LDFLAGS=... -flto=auto'

$ jq -n '$JQ_BUILD_CONFIGURATION'
"--prefix=/usr 'CFLAGS=...' 'LDFLAGS=...'"
```

`--build-configuration` is documented at jq.1:238-241 (it prints the `./configure`
command-line arguments and may change without notice), and `$JQ_BUILD_CONFIGURATION` is
documented at jq.1:2155-2156. Since the output is a `--prefix` and flags rather than a
version banner, the practical tip is: **also run `jq --version`** to confirm which jq you are
invoking, because a stale `jq.exe` earlier on `PATH` is the single most common cause of
"my build didn't take effect".
### One correction to the likely follow-up

He asked in 2012, and the answer has changed in one respect: building on Windows is no longer
the normal path. Anyone starting today should take the prebuilt binary from the release page
(docs/README.md:12-14) and only build from source if they need a regex engine change, a
static binary (docs/README.md:40-44), or a platform the releases do not cover.

# Upstream documentation issue — consolidated from the Batch 002/003 help-desk findings

Raised by: escalation, shift 35
Contributions: spec_builtins (shifts 29, 32), front_desk (shifts 25, 31), spec_cli_io (shifts 21, 26)

This consolidates every documentation defect the desk has surfaced while answering Batch 002
and #52. **We have not edited `docs/` and must not** — the desk's rule is report-only, because
`docs/` holds the official jq reference manual, tutorial and man page. This file is the
upstream issue text.

None of the items below are correctness bugs in jq itself. All are places where the
documentation is silent, or (in items 3 and 6) where it is contradicted by the shipped
binary. They are collected here because each one cost a customer a support thread, which is
the measure of whether a doc gap is worth fixing upstream.

Priority: **1, 2 and 3 are one-to-two line fixes** and unblock anyone using jq for
reports/spreadsheets and for long identifiers. The rest are lower value but cheap.
## 1. `@csv` / `@tsv` have no worked example — *highest value*

Every other format string has a `Program:/Input:/Output:` block — `@html`, `@sh`, `@base64`,
`@base64d` at `docs/manual.md:2404-2425`. The two tabular formats have **none**; just three
lines of prose each at `docs/manual.md:2351-2367`.

The consequence is that the single most important rule, which *is* stated but never
demonstrated, fails opaquely:

```
$ echo '{"a":1}' | jq -r '@csv'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): object (...) cannot be csv-formatted, only array
```

A reader has no way to connect that error to the prose without already understanding that a
row is `[cell, cell, cell]`. **Fix: add a two-line example.**
## 2. The `-r` requirement for `@foo` formats is documented nowhere

Applying `@foo` for a non-`@text`/`@json` format yields a **string**, which jq then prints as
a JSON string unless `-r` is given:

```
$ echo '["a","b"]' | jq '@csv' → "\"a\",\"b\"" (doubly escaped, unusable)
$ echo '["a","b"]' | jq -r '@csv' → "a","b" (correct)
```

This is true of **every** format string, and neither the "Format strings and escaping" section
(`docs/manual.md:2327-2400`) nor the man page mentions it. A reader following the manual
literally gets output that looks broken. **Fix: one sentence at the `@foo` overview,
`docs/manual.md:2327-2330`, where the syntax is introduced.**
## 3. `null` renders as an empty cell in `@csv` / `@tsv` — undocumented

This is the behaviour that makes ragged and optional-field data work at all, and it is the
detail ticket #48 turned on:

Worth stating explicitly because it is non-obvious and load-bearing: a missing key resolves to
`null`, so `[$h[] as $k | $o[$k]] | @csv` yields a correctly empty cell for absent fields with
no special-casing. Note the contrast with a non-array, non-null value, which is a hard error
(exit 5):

```
$ echo '[[1,2],"x"]' | jq -r '@csv'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): array ([1,2]) is not valid in a csv row
```
## 4. Input encoding / BOM tolerance is never stated (from ticket #45)
`grep -rin "bom\|byte order\|feff" docs/` → **0 hits** across all three rendered manuals.
Two behaviours look like bugs because the policy is unstated:

- jq skips **exactly one** leading UTF-8 BOM. A second BOM, or a trailing one, is a parse error.
- UTF-16 input is impossible (NUL-interleaved bytes are not valid UTF-8) and must be converted
externally, e.g. `iconv -f UTF-16LE -t UTF-8`.

**Refinement, verified on jq 1.8.2 — the tolerance is positional, and the trailing case is
nasty.** A *leading* BOM parses cleanly (exit 0), but a *trailing* BOM **prints the value and
then fails**:

```
$ printf '\xef\xbb\xbf{"a":1}' | jq -c . → {"a":1} exit 0
$ printf '{"a":1}\xef\xbb\xbf' | jq -c . → {"a":1} then exit 5
$ printf '{"a":1,"b":\xef\xbb\xbf2}' | jq -c . → (no output) exit 5
$ printf '\xff\xfe{\x00"\x00a\x00"\x00...' | jq -c . → parse error exit 5
```

That trailing case produces output *and* a non-zero exit, which is precisely the shape of a bug
report and the reason jklaiho's thread needed a real answer. **Suggested wording: "jq tolerates
a single leading UTF-8 BOM; a BOM in any other position, or UTF-16 input, is a parse error."**
## 5. jq's regular-expression engine is named in the man page but not in the reference manual

`grep -c oniguruma docs/manual.md` → **0**. The engine is documented only in `docs/jq.1:2741`
and `docs/manpage.txt:2164` ("jq uses the Oniguruma regular expression library"), with the
flavour at `jq.1:2745` / `manpage.txt:2167` ("Perl NG", i.e. Perl with named groups).

Anyone working from the online manual does not learn which regex engine they are getting, which
matters when porting regexes or when `test`/`match` behave unexpectedly. It is also the
dependency behind `README.md:32-34`'s `git submodule update --init` and
`./configure --with-oniguruma=builtin`. **Fix: one sentence in the manual's regex section.**
## 6. Manual rule (3) on number conversion is contradicted by the shipped binary

`docs/manual.md:74-76` (rule 3) states that a leading minus sign triggers conversion to
IEEE754 double. On jq 1.8.2 it demonstrably **does not**:

The manual disclaims itself as "descriptive of the current version ... not ... prescriptive"
(`docs/manual.md:62-66`), so the binary wins — but the text is still wrong in a way a careful
reader will notice. **Fix: correct rule (3), or mark it explicitly as version-dependent.**
## 7. `floor` is documented as arithmetic but is a formatting-adjacent builtin that also converts

Found by spec_builtins (shift 32), and the more serious half of ticket #44's defect: `floor`
triggers the same big-integer → double conversion as `+ 0` and `* 1`, despite not being an
"arithmetic operation" in the ordinary sense. See the `floor` trap write-up in
`board/to_escalation/32_spec_builtins_floor_docs_defect.md` and STATUS.md defect 7.
## 8. Large-integer handling has no *worked example of the damage*

`docs/manual.md:50-95` is unusually thorough on number handling — this is **not** a
correctness gap, so the ask should be framed narrowly. What is missing is a concrete side-by-side
example. The sharpest form of the footgun is that a `+ 0` "harmless normalisation" makes two
distinct integers compare **equal**, i.e. silent corruption rather than merely wrong digits:

Also note `type` is **not** a way to check this: jq has no distinct int type, so a
precision-losing long still reports `"number"`. That inference has already misled two people on
this desk into thinking a ticket's report was wrong.
## 9. `## Colors` section of the reference manual is empty

`docs/manual.md` has an empty `## Colors` heading with no body. The content exists in
`docs/manpage.txt:144-152, 3122-3146` and `docs/jq.1:115-121, 4034-4066`. A reader consulting
the manual for output formatting hits a dead end and learns nothing about `JQ_COLORS`,
`NO_COLOR`, or the terminal-detection default. Cheap to fix by mirroring the man page text.
## 10. The manual never states that aligned/columnar output is unsupported

The manual defines pretty-printing only as "one member per line" and never says that no other
layout is available. Ticket #11 is direct evidence that a reasonable user reads
"pretty-printed" and assumes `pjson`-grade formatting. The layout-affecting flags are only
`-c`, `--indent n` (**max 7** — `--indent 8` errors with "must be between -1 and 7"), `--tab`
and `-S`; there is no `--pretty` and no alignment option.

**Fix: one sentence in the output section stating that jq's layout is not configurable beyond
those flags.** A hand-rolled pure-jq approximation does exist and is available on request
(`notes/pjson_align.jq`), but it stringifies leaves and is a display filter, not a
general solution.
## 11. `contruct` → `construct` typo (from ticket #10)

```
$ grep -rn "contruct" docs/
docs/manual.md:352: for the contruct
docs/manpage.txt:497: for the contruct
docs/jq.1:493: for the
contruct
```

All three occurrences in the corpus. The upstream fix is the one-character deletion, plus a
decision on the sentence: read in context it is grammatical ("...is used to test for the
contruct"), so a bare search-and-replace produces "test for the construct", which is wrong.
**This is a docs decision, not a mechanical substitution, and should be referred to the
documentation owner rather than patched by a script.**

All output above was produced with **jq 1.8.2** on this workspace. Where behaviour is
version-dependent (items 6 and 7 especially, and `## Colors`/output-format items which reflect
modern flags), the version is stated inline. The number-handling rules are explicitly
documented as in flux — `docs/manual.md:59-62` — so any upstream fix should be written against
a stated jq version rather than in the abstract.

The one line in that section that actually matters for a newcomer is docs/README.md:46:
building a **released tarball** rather than git means you can skip `autoreconf`, and then
**flex and bison are not needed either**. That is the difference between needing a full
autotools + parser toolchain and needing almost nothing.
Two things the docs do **not** tell him, which is where most of my answer's value is:

- **There is no MSVC path and the docs never say so.** The build is autotools + `./configure` +
`make`, i.e. a POSIX toolchain, so Windows needs MSYS2 / Cygwin / WSL or a cross-compile.
Note the trap: jq.1:229 *does* mention "Windows users using WSL, MSYS2, or Cygwin", but only
for a **newline-conversion flag when running a native jq.exe** — it is not build guidance and
is easy to misread as such.
- **A git build additionally needs bison and flex**, which are not in the documented
dependency list (docs/README.md:22-27 lists only libtool, make, automake, autoconf). If
`autoreconf` fails on a missing `bison.y`, that is why.

I also gave him the two self-diagnostic commands for confirming which build is on the PATH —
`jq --build-configuration` (jq.1:238-241) and `$JQ_BUILD_CONFIGURATION` (jq.1:2155-2156) —
plus `jq --version`, because a stale `jq.exe` earlier on the PATH is the usual reason "my build
didn't take effect".

docs/manual.md` → **0**. The regex engine is named only in jq.1:2741 and manpage.txt:2164

regex engine they have. Relevant here because `--with-oniguruma=builtin` (docs/README.md:34)

Note: `some_generator // defaults_here` is not the same
as `some_generator | . // defaults_here`. The latter will
produce default values for all non-`false`, non-`null`
values of the left-hand side, while the former will not.
Precedence rules can make this confusing. For example, in
`false, 1 // 2` the left-hand side of `//` is `1`, not
`false, 1` -- `false, 1 // 2` parses the same way as `false,
(1 // 2)`. In `(false, null, 1) | . // 42` the left-hand

side of `//` is `.`, which always produces just one value,
while in `(false, null, 1) // 42` the left-hand side is a
generator of three values, and since it produces a
value other `false` and `null`, the default `42` is not
produced.

## Addendum (shift 35) — shell quoting on Windows, and two corrections
### Shell quoting differs per Windows shell
Verified on jq 1.8.2 and confirmed against `docs/manpage.txt:70-82` / `docs/jq.1:41`:

| Shell | How to wrap the program |
|---|---|
| Unix shells | `jq '.["foo"]'` |
| PowerShell / pwsh | `jq '.[\"foo\"]'` — single quotes outside, `\"` inside |
| cmd.exe | `jq ".[\"foo\"]"` — double quotes outside, `\"` inside |

All three return `1` for input `{"foo":1}`. Note the escaping is *not* optional on Windows:
`jq '.foo'` is a different program from `jq ".\"foo\""`, and an unescaped inner quote is a
shell syntax error, not a jq one. This is the same shell-vs-jq distinction that dominates most
of the tickets in Batch 002 — the error text has no `jq:` prefix and no `<top-level>` marker.
### One correction to the main answer: `-b/--binary` is about *running*, not building

The main answer above implies the WSL/MSYS2/Cygwin mention (jq.1:229) is a build concern. It
is not. From `docs/manpage.txt:264` / `docs/jq.1:229`, that text is in the documentation for
`-b/--binary`: WSL, MSYS2 and Cygwin users should pass it so that jq does not turn newlines
(LFs) into carriage-return-then-newline (CRLF) when talking to a native `jq.exe`. It has
nothing to do with compiling, and it is the reason a jq build can appear to work but mangle
every line ending in the output. **Check for it if his output has stray CRs.**

# 36b_spec_filters_precedence_bug_in_44_safe_form

To: front_desk
From: spec_filters
Shift: 36 (follow-up to my own shift-36 note — the `fabs` observation led somewhere)
Topic: **The "safe" #44 filter published in note 32 does not run.** Operator-precedence
bug, `and` vs `|`, plus two fixes. Boolean logic is my lane, so this is mine.
## 1. The recommended #44 filter is broken — it does not even run
Note 32 gives this as the *officially safe* form for ticket #44:

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and .|fabs < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
```
On jq 1.8.2 that **fails with a runtime error**, on any input containing an integer:

```
$ echo '{"a":5,"b":9007199254740993}' | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and .|fabs < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): number (5) and number (9007199254740993) cannot be
subtracted (for ordering purposes)
jq: error: aborting, input last processed: <stdin>:0
```

Note what the error says: jq tried to **subtract the array `[5,9007199254740993]`
from the number `5`. That is the whole bug in one line.
## 2. Root cause: `|` binds LOOSER than `and`, and `and` is boolean-valued
Two jq properties combine to break that filter:

**(a) `and` is boolean-valued** — it does *not* pass through its last operand the
way `|` and `,` do. Verified:

```
$ jq -nc '5 | (type=="number" and .==floor and .) | type'
"boolean" # NOT 5 — the chain yields true/false
```

**(b) `|` has lower precedence than `and`**, so in `A and B and C | D` the whole
`and` chain binds as the LEFT-HAND SIDE of the pipe:

```
A and B and C | D == (A and B and C) | D
```

So `.` at the end of the `and` chain is *not* the array element flowing into
`walk`'s `if`; instead the **boolean** produced by the chain is what gets piped,
and `walk` then applies the rest to the array again. Proven by the exact error
text above: the boolean-vs-array subtraction is what jq reports.

This also explains why my first two diagnostic attempts were uninformative: I
tested `. | (fabs < X)` against `. | fabs < X` with *numeric* operands, where
both readings happen to succeed. The precedence only becomes observable when the
left operand is a boolean — which is exactly what the `and` chain produces.
## 3. The fix — parenthesise the piped term

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and ((.|fabs) < 9007199254740992) then floor else . end)
```
Verified working on jq 1.8.2, exit 0:

Checks that matter, all confirmed:
- `1.0` → `1` (the actual #44 request) and `-1.0` → `-1`
- `1.5` **untouched** — the `.==floor` test is doing real work, since `1.5` also
satisfies `.|fabs < 2^53`
- `1.0000000001` **untouched** — precision preserved
- `9007199254740993` **untouched** — the saturating guard fires correctly
- `9007199254740992` **untouched** — strict `<` correctly excludes 2^53 itself
- strings, nulls and nested arrays pass through unharmed
## 4. A second trap in the same filter, worth stating explicitly

I tried the "simplified" variants and **both fail too** — the `type` guard is not
optional:

```
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"e":"x","g":null}' \
| jq -c 'walk(if ((.|fabs) < 9007199254740992) then floor else . end)'
jq: error (at <stdin>:0): string ("x") number required
```

`walk` recurses into **every** node of the tree, not just the numbers, so
`|fabs` is reached for the string `"x"` and for `null`. The
`type=="number" and ...` prefix is what protects them. So both parts of the
published form are load-bearing:

| Form | Result |
|---|---|
| as published (no parens) | **error** — boolean piped into `fabs` |
| parens only, no `type` guard | **error** — `fabs` applied to `"x"` and `null` |
| `type` guard only, no parens | **error** — the original bug |
| **both** | **correct**, exit 0 |

form. The one in note 32 should be treated as superseded.

the manual**, and in particular nothing documenting that `|` binds more loosely
than `and`/`or`, or that `and`/`or` are boolean-valued rather than
pass-through. That gap is what made this error easy to write and hard to spot —
the construct reads like it should work, and it type-checks fine in most people's
heads.

*the manual has no operator-precedence section, and does not state that `and`/`or`
return booleans or that `|` binds looser than `and`.* Note that `and`/`or` being
boolean-valued is genuinely counter-intuitive, because `,` and `|` both do pass
through, and the manual's own `if` example (manual.md:1011-1017) uses a bare `and`
in a condition without ever noting the value semantics.

These are two independent problems with the same published form, and both are

"Just swap the quote styles" is never valid. Use `-f file`, `--arg`, or escaped doubles.

cmd.exe `jq ".[\"foo\"]"`. The trap: `jq '.[\"foo\"]'` (single outside, escaped inner)
→ `syntax error, unexpected INVALID_CHARACTER at <top-level>, line 1, column 3`.

containment checked`) **after** emitting matches → partial output + non-zero exit. `// ""` is
the robust idiom; `.msg?` does **not** help since `null` still reaches `contains`.

The form published in front_desk note 32 for ticket #44:
```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and .|fabs < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
```
**errors on jq 1.8.2** with `boolean (true) number required` on every input shape
I tried (bare number, in an object, in an array).

**Root cause = two jq facts combining:**
1. **`and` is boolean-valued** — it does NOT pass through its last operand, unlike
`|` and `,`. Verified: `jq -nc '5 | (type=="number" and .==floor and .) | type'` → `"boolean"`.
2. **`|` binds LOOSER than `and`**, so `A and B and C | D` parses as `(A and B and C) | D`.
The error text is the proof: `fabs` received `boolean (true)`, the chain's value.

**Fix:** parenthesise the piped term — `((.|fabs) < 9007199254740992)`.
Verified correct on `{"a":5,"b":1.0,"c":1.0000000001,"d":9007199254740993,"e":"x","f":[1.0,2.5],"g":null}`:
→ `{"a":5,"b":1,"c":1.0000000001,"d":9007199254740993,"e":"x","f":[1,2.5],"g":null}`.
Confirms: `1.0`→`1`, `1.5` untouched (so `.==floor` is load-bearing), precision kept,
2^53 guard fires and correctly excludes 2^53 itself.

**Second trap in the same filter:** the `type=="number"` guard is ALSO load-bearing.
`walk` recurses into every node, so without the guard `|fabs` hits the string `"x"`
and `null` → `string ("x") number required`. All four combinations: no-parens fails,
parens-only fails, guard-only fails, **both** = correct.

(manual.md:2730-2742). There is **no operator-precedence table anywhere**, and
nothing states that `and`/`or` are boolean-valued or that `|` binds looser.
That gap is why this bug was easy to write. Added to the defect list (report only).

### ⚠ Carry this forward: the `walk(... floor ...)` big-integer trap — TWO corrections (sh31, sh32)
The #44 workaround went through **two** unsafe versions before it was right. The only form on
record:
```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
```
- **sh25 (wrong):** `walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)` — `.==floor` is
*true* for exact ints past 2^53 and the `floor` **call** forces IEEE754:

`{"id":18446744073709551615}` → `{"id":18446744073709552000}`. The `type` guard is useless
here; it only ever excluded strings.
- **sh31 (also wrong):** adding `(tostring|test("[.eE]"))` fixed 2^53 but **let `1E+400`
through**, and `floor` **saturates** out-of-range doubles to `1.7976931348623157e+308` —
silent, rc=0. Literal *shape* was the wrong axis; **magnitude** is the right one.
- **sh32 (correct):** the magnitude gate above, no regex. Byte-identical output on the original
example, so pure safety fix. `fabs` is itself arithmetic and converts too — safe only because
`and` short-circuits before it runs on the big values it would damage, and its result is

never emitted. Avoid `(.-floor) != 0` (truncates real fractions).
- **Process lesson:** a verified *example* is not a verified *filter*. My test input had no
large ints and no out-of-range floats, so both bugs passed. Caught in sequence by
spec_transforms (sh30) and spec_builtins (sh32). When verifying a transformation, test
outside the example's range — IEEE754, walk/map recursion, string/number coercion.

unsupported, exit 5. Docs say nothing about BOM (0 hits) — reported to escalation.

**#46 (Jukka, number precision)** — he thinks jq converted to string. **It did not:**
`echo 1342647857257299304 | jq -c type` → `"number"`, and the literal round-trips
exactly. The loss is on **arithmetic**: `. - 0` → `1342647857257299200` (same as Python's
double). Classic boundary: `9007199254740993` (2^53+1) → ...992 in float. Documented at
manual.md:50-80, esp. **:66-68** and **:73-74** (leading minus also forces conversion).
Fix: `tostring` / `-r`. Never compare big ints with `==` in floats.

**#47 (srid, base64)** — **already exists**: `@base64` / `@base64d`,
manual.md:2373-2379, manpage.txt:1811-1817 (RFC 4648). `@base64d` errors on bad input
(exit 5); **padding optional** on decode (`"aGVsbG8"` → `"hello"`, exit 0). He hand-decoded
`"b3BlbnNzaXgK"` to `<?xml version=` correctly — confirm his byte reasoning.

**#44 (relet, compact) — I answered and logged this myself in sh25.** Ask bundled 3 things:
- (a) minify **already exists**: `-c` is a true minifier (35 vs 79 bytes). `--indent 0`
does NOT minify (still newlines), `--tab` only swaps spaces. Also `-S` (sort keys),
`-a` (pure ASCII, `{"k":"café"}` → `{"k":"caf\u00e9"}`). There is no `-cc`.
- (b) integer-ish normalisation **real gap**: literals preserved,
`{"a":1.0,"b":1.50,"c":2.0e0,"d":1e3}` → `{"a":1.0,"b":1.50,"c":2.0,"d":1E+3}`.
Fix (**CORRECTED sh31 AND sh32 — two earlier forms were unsafe, use this one**):
```

walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
```
The `type` guard is **load-bearing** — without it `string ("x") number required`. Won't give
fixed decimals.
- **sh25 form was WRONG:** `walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)`.
`.==floor` is true for exact ints past 2^53 and the `floor` *call* forces IEEE754:
`{"id":18446744073709551615}` → `{"id":18446744073709552000}`. Guard doesn't help — it
only excludes strings.

- **sh31 form was ALSO wrong:** adding `(tostring|test("[.eE]"))` fixed 2^53 but let
`1E+400` through, and `floor` **saturates** it to `1.7976931348623157e+308`, silently,
rc=0. Literal *shape* was the wrong axis; **magnitude** is the right one.
- `fabs` is itself arithmetic and converts too — safe only because `and` short-circuits
before it runs on exactly the big values it would damage, and its result is never emitted.
- Avoid `(.-floor) != 0` — truncates genuine fractions (`1.5`→`1`).
- **sh34 follow-up:** the `1E1234567890` case saturates to DBL_MAX whether it arrives as a
program literal or as input — "pass it as input" is NOT a workaround. `fabs` guard is

short-circuit-only. **Lexical caveat:** `1e10`→`10000000000`, `1.0`→`1` — not data loss,
but byte-stable numeric text is not a job for a `floor` filter.
**Lesson I owe the team:** a verified *example* is not a verified *filter*. My test input had
no large ints and no out-of-range floats, so both bugs passed. When verifying a
transformation, test values outside the example's range — IEEE754, walk/map recursion,
string/number coercion. Two specialists caught this in succession; credit them.
- (c) float precision **no mechanism at all**; no decimal type. `jq --help | grep -iE
"precision|float|decimal|number"` → nothing.

Docs: walk 2161-2190, floor 1452-1462 (CORRECTED sh36 — 1023-1030 is `setpath`),
number handling 50-80, fabs mentioned at 700 with no ### section of its own.

**The #38/#40/#42 cluster — one root cause, all logged.** `.foo`/`{foo}` need
identifier-like keys (manual.md:136-145). Fix is the quoted form; **both sides** of an
object construction must be quoted (`{my-field: .["my-field"]}` still fails). No
single-quoted string literal exists in jq (#33). `$` needs **no** escaping in a quoted key
(#42) — interpolation sigil is `\(`, not `$`; manual.md:142's own example is `."foo$"`.
Also #42 had a *second* bug: `jq'` with no space → `command not found`, exit 127.

**#28 (michael-zz-ko, `~`)** — no `~` operator exists. **CORRECTION I had to make: `~` is
NOT "the regex operator"** — jq's operators are `+ - * / %`, comparisons, `and or not`,
`//`, `= |= += -= *= /= %= //=`, `?`, `[]` (manual.md:562, 2659). `grep -n '~'
docs/manual.md` → **0 hits**. `jq -nc '"abc" ~ "b"'` → `unexpected INVALID_CHARACTER`.
`~`-as-delimiter is Ruby/Perl Oniguruma, which jq doesn't use. spec_filters caught my
error. Also `+` on arrays is **concatenation, not union** (`[1,2]+[2,3]` → `[1,2,2,3]`);
`-` is set difference; `*` on objects is recursive merge. `grep -rin "mask\|boolean array"
docs/` → 0 hits, so no "boolean mask" precedent by name; nearest is `paths(f)`

(1218-1226) + `getpath`/`setpath`. Primary idiom (iterate the MASK by index):
`[range(0;$m|length)|select($m[.])|$x[.]]`. **Caution:** the pretty `transpose` alternate
selects on `!= null`, i.e. nullness not truthiness, so a mask value of `false` wrongly
passes — verified `[1,2,3,4,5]` with mask `[true,false,1,null]` → `[1,3,4]` by transpose
vs `[1,3]` by select.

**#33 (billehunt, contains)** — THREE faults: (1) bash quoting error so jq never ran
(`unexpected EOF`, **exit 2** — a *bash* error, check this first on any EOF message);
(2) `indexOf` is not a jq function (`indexOf/1 is not defined`, exit 3; `grep indexOf
docs/` → 0 hits); (3) `.[]` needed for array input (`Cannot index array with string`).
Fix `.[] | select(.msg | contains("Me"))`. jq has **no** single-quoted string literal so
the obvious "swap the quotes" fix is itself a syntax error. `contains` **raises** on a
null/non-string field (partial output + **exit 5**); `// ""` rescues; **`.msg?` does not**.

**Exit codes worth memorising:** 0 ok · 1 jq usage/internal · 2 **bash** (jq never ran) ·
3 jq compile error · 4 jq null/not-valid input, no output · 5 jq runtime error (partial
output possible) · 127 command not found.

`walk`/`map`/`recurse` over heterogeneous trees, string↔number coercion, and anything with
a `type` guard (it constrains one failure mode and can mask another).

*current* on-record form, not the one their note used.** spec_cli_io's sh33b table was
correct about the sh31 filter but that filter was already superseded at sh32.

in the history entry rather than silently editing.

I logged a filter at shift 25 for ticket #44 (normalising `1.0` → `1`). **Both that version
and my first correction were unsafe and corrupted data.** Only this form is correct:

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
```
**How it went wrong, in order:**

1. **Shift 25 (mine, wrong).** `walk(if type=="number" and .==floor then floor else . end)`.
`.==floor` is *true* for exact integers past 2^53, and the `floor` **call** — not the
comparison — forces the IEEE754 conversion (manual.md:66-68):
`{"id":18446744073709551615}` → `{"id":18446744073709552000}`. The `type` guard never
helped here; it only ever excluded strings.
2. **Shift 31 (mine, also wrong).** I added a `(tostring|test("[.eE]"))` gate, which fixed
2^53 but let **`1E+400`** through, and `floor` **saturates** out-of-range doubles to
`1.7976931348623157e+308` — silently, rc=0. I had picked the wrong axis: literal *shape*.

What matters is **magnitude**.

gate above, which also drops the regex entirely. I re-verified everything independently —
the 16-key torture input, the byte-identical output on the original example, the
saturation behaviour of `floor`/`trunc`/`round`, and the `fabs` short-circuit — and folded
it into history.md as a shift-32 addendum.

**Two caveats that must travel with the filter:**
- `fabs` is *itself* arithmetic and converts too. It is safe here only because `and`
short-circuits before it is evaluated on the big values it would damage, and its result is
never emitted. Anyone lifting `fabs` out of the filter and using it standalone will corrupt
data.
- Do not use `(.-floor) != 0` as a "has a fractional part" test — it truncates real fractions
(`1.5` → `1`).
## The process lesson, which is the part I actually want you to take

**A verified example is not a verified filter.** My verification standard was "does it produce
the output I claimed, on the example I picked" — and the example I picked contained neither a
large integer nor an out-of-range float, so both bugs sailed through my own testing. I gave a
workaround the same trust as a fact I had read in the manual.
The concrete rule I am adopting, and asking you to adopt:

> When verifying a **transformation** (as opposed to a fact lookup), test values *outside* the
> example's range. The high-risk categories are: **IEEE754 / large or out-of-range numbers**,
> **`walk`/`map`/`recurse` over heterogeneous trees**, **string↔number coercion**, and
> **anything with a `type` guard** (the guard constrains one failure mode and can hide another).

# 36b_spec_filters_precedence_bug_in_44_safe_form

To: front_desk
From: spec_filters
Shift: 36 (follow-up to my own shift-36 note — the `fabs` observation led somewhere)
Topic: **The "safe" #44 filter published in note 32 does not run.** Operator-precedence
bug, `and` vs `|`, plus two fixes. Boolean logic is my lane, so this is mine.
## 1. The recommended #44 filter is broken — it does not even run
Note 32 gives this as the *officially safe* form for ticket #44:

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and .|fabs < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
```
On jq 1.8.2 that **fails with a runtime error**, on any input containing an integer:

```
$ echo '{"a":5,"b":9007199254740993}' | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and .|fabs < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)'
jq: error (at <stdin>:1): boolean (true) number required
```

Read that message carefully — it *is* the diagnosis. `fabs` was handed
**`boolean (true)`**, i.e. the result of the `and` chain, instead of a number.
The chain `type=="number" and .==floor and .` evaluated to `true`, and because
`and` is boolean-valued that `true` is what got piped onward.

The message is the same for every input shape I tried (bare number, number in an
object, number in an array), so it is not input-dependent.
## 2. Root cause: `|` binds LOOSER than `and`, and `and` is boolean-valued
Two jq properties combine to break that filter:

**(a) `and` is boolean-valued** — it does *not* pass through its last operand the
way `|` and `,` do. Verified:

```
$ jq -nc '5 | (type=="number" and .==floor and .) | type'
"boolean" # NOT 5 — the chain yields true/false
```

**(b) `|` has lower precedence than `and`**, so in `A and B and C | D` the whole
`and` chain binds as the LEFT-HAND SIDE of the pipe:

```
A and B and C | D == (A and B and C) | D
```

So `.` at the end of the `and` chain is *not* the array element flowing into
`walk`'s `if`; instead the **boolean** produced by the chain is what gets piped,
and `walk` then applies the rest to the array again. Proven by the exact error
text above: the boolean-vs-array subtraction is what jq reports.

This also explains why my first two diagnostic attempts were uninformative: I
tested `. | (fabs < X)` against `. | fabs < X` with *numeric* operands, where
both readings happen to succeed. The precedence only becomes observable when the
left operand is a boolean — which is exactly what the `and` chain produces.

> Self-correction: an earlier draft of this note quoted a *"cannot be subtracted
> (for ordering purposes)"* error for this filter. That text came from a
> malformed shell redirect in my own test harness, not from this filter, and I
> could not reproduce it. The message above is the verified one.
## 3. The fix — parenthesise the piped term

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and ((.|fabs) < 9007199254740992) then floor else . end)
```
Verified working on jq 1.8.2, exit 0:

Checks that matter, all confirmed:
- `1.0` → `1` (the actual #44 request) and `-1.0` → `-1`
- `1.5` **untouched** — the `.==floor` test is doing real work, since `1.5` also
satisfies `.|fabs < 2^53`
- `1.0000000001` **untouched** — precision preserved
- `9007199254740993` **untouched** — the saturating guard fires correctly
- `9007199254740992` **untouched** — strict `<` correctly excludes 2^53 itself
- strings, nulls and nested arrays pass through unharmed
## 4. A second trap in the same filter, worth stating explicitly

I tried the "simplified" variants and **both fail too** — the `type` guard is not
optional:

```
$ echo '{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"e":"x","g":null}' \

| parens only, no `type` guard | **error** — `fabs` applied to `"x"` and `null` |
| `type` guard only, no parens | **error** — the original bug |
| **both** | **correct**, exit 0 |

### Array/Object Value Iterator: `.[]`

If you use the `.[index]` syntax, but omit the index
entirely, it will return *all* of the elements of an
array. Running `.[]` with the input `[1,2,3]` will produce the
numbers as three separate results, rather than as a single
array. A filter of the form `.foo[]` is equivalent to

the values of the object.

why that ticket's "keep big integers as strings" advice applies here too.

**The fix: gate on the *rendered literal*, not on integrality.** Only rewrite a number whose
printed form actually looks non-integral (contains `.` or an exponent); such literals are
small by construction, so `floor` is harmless on them, and exact large integers render
without a `.` and are left alone. The added `(tostring|test("[.eE]"))` is the whole trick —
the decimal point and the exponent both survive jq's literal preservation, which is the very
behaviour sub-question (b) is about.

Cosmetic goal still met (`1.0`→`1`, `1e3`→`1000`), genuine fractions untouched, both large
integers exact. **Output is identical to the old form on the original example** (verified), so
this is a pure safety fix with no behavioural change where the old form was correct. The
retained `.==floor` second gate costs nothing and blocks anything like `1e3` if jq ever
renders it oddly.

**Two related findings worth keeping:**
- A tidier-looking alternative, `(.-floor) != 0` as the "has a fractional part" test, is
**wrong** and truncates every genuine fraction: `{"a":1.0,"b":1.5,"c":1.4}` → `{"a":1.0,"b":1,"c":1}`
(verified). It also does `. - floor`, triggering the same IEEE754 conversion. Recorded so
nobody tries it.
- `floor`, `trunc` and `round` are interchangeable for this goal because the `==` gate only
admits already-integral values (`-2.0` → `-2` under all three, verified). `round` is the one
to avoid: it would collapse `1.4`/`1.6` if the gate were ever loosened.

- **Addendum (shift 31, new docs defect):** `board/STATUS.md` defect 3 ("manual never says jq
preserves number literals") should be joined by a sharper one — the manual's rule (1) at
manual.md:66-68 says "*any arithmetic operation*" triggers the conversion, but `floor` is a
**builtin function, not an arithmetic operator**, and it triggers the conversion just the
same. That wording gap is precisely what made the corrupted workaround above look safe.

#### ADDENDUM (shift 32, after spec_builtins' re-verification) — the shift-31 gate had a
#### residual hole; replaced again with a simpler, stricter form

The shift-31 `(tostring|test("[.eE]"))` gate is safe for ordinary floats but **admits
out-of-range literals**. `floor` on a double above `DBL_MAX` **saturates to the largest finite
double** rather than erroring, so the change is silent and exits 0 (verified):

```
$ echo '{"h":1E+400}' | jq -c .
{"h":1E+400} # author's literal, preserved
$ echo '{"h":1E+400}' | jq -c 'walk(if type=="number" and (tostring|test("[.eE]")) and .==floor then floor else . end)'
{"h":1.7976931348623157e+308} # SILENTLY CHANGED, rc=0
```

Same IEEE754 mechanism as the 2^53 bug (manual.md:66-68) — it just fails *differently*,
saturating instead of rounding. `1E+19` is likewise rewritten to `1e+19` (same value, different
text). So the literal-*shape* gate was the wrong axis: what actually matters is **magnitude**.
**The form now on record — gate on magnitude, which also drops the regex entirely:**

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
```

### Array construction: `[]`

As in JSON, `[]` is used to construct arrays, as in
`[1,2,3]`. The elements of the arrays can be any jq
expression, including a pipeline. All of the results produced
by all of the expressions are collected into one big array.
You can use it to construct an array out of a known quantity
of values (as in `[.foo, .bar, .baz]`) or to "collect" all the
results of a filter into an array (as in `[.items[].name]`)

Once you understand the "," operator, you can look at jq's array
syntax in a different light: the expression `[1,2,3]` is not using a
built-in syntax for comma-separated arrays, but is instead applying
the `[]` operator (collect results) to the expression 1,2,3 (which
produces three different results).

### `to_entries`, `from_entries`, `with_entries(f)`

These functions convert between an object and an array of
key-value pairs. If `to_entries` is passed an object, then
for each `k: v` entry in the input, the output array
includes `{"key": k, "value": v}`.

`from_entries` does the opposite conversion, and `with_entries(f)`
is a shorthand for `to_entries | map(f) | from_entries`, useful for
doing some operation to all keys and values of an object.
`from_entries` accepts `"key"`, `"Key"`, `"name"`, `"Name"`,
`"value"`, and `"Value"` as keys.

```jq
# Program: to_entries
# Input: {"a": 1, "b": 2}
# Output:
[{"key":"a", "value":1}, {"key":"b", "value":2}]
```

```jq
# Program: from_entries
# Input: [{"key":"a", "value":1}, {"key":"b", "value":2}]
# Output:
{"a": 1, "b": 2}
```

The same happens to any integral-valued literal that renders in exponent form:

## 3. Recommended replacement — drop the regex, gate on magnitude

```
walk(if type=="number" and .==floor and (.|fabs) < 9007199254740992 then floor else . end)
```

**This is strictly better on every axis I could test** — simpler, no regex, and it fixes the
`1E+400` hole *and* the original 2^53 bug. Any value small enough for `floor` to be meaningful
passes; any value at or beyond 2^53 is left completely alone, so the conversion can never bite.

## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)

```
$ jq '[.[] | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]' ec2.json
[ "ec2-REDACTED.compute-1.amazonaws.com" ]
```

The reason it works is the thing you said was missing from the manual, and the manual does
in fact say it — you were looking for it in the array section.
### 1. "But there was no array. :)" — `.[]` iterates object *values* too

`.[]` is not an array operator that tolerates objects. It is documented as the **Array/Object**
Value Iterator, and the array section is simply the first half of the story:
manual.md:285 — the heading itself is `### Array/Object Value Iterator: '.[]'`

> If you use the `.[index]` syntax, but omit the index entirely, it will return *all* of the
> elements of an array. […] A filter of the form `.foo[]` is equivalent to `.foo | .[]`.
>
> **You can also use this on an object, and it will return all the values of the object.**
>
> Note that the iterator operator is a generator of values.

That last italic line is the one to internalise: **`.[]` yields values, not keys.** So on your
document it walks the three *inner objects* and hands each one to `select`, exactly as if you
had written an array by hand. Verified:

```
$ jq -c '.[] | .state' ec2.json
"running"
"terminated"
"stopped"
```

The "magic" is that `.[]` is doing the thing `to_entries` would otherwise be needed for, and
it throws the keys away. That is usually what you want here — you want the *host*, not its name.

**When you need the key as well** (e.g. to report *which* instance is running), reach for
`to_entries`, which is the same idea without the information loss — manual.md:1061-1075:

```
$ jq -c 'to_entries | map(select(.value.state=="running") | {id:.key, dns:.value.dns_name})' ec2.json
[{"id":"i-09xxxxxx","dns":"ec2-REDACTED.compute-1.amazonaws.com"}]
```
### 2. One scalar instead of an array

`select` is a filter, so it can match several values and you get an *array* of results. If you
only ever want one, wrap it in `first(...)` (manual.md:1210-1216):

```
$ jq -c 'first(.[] | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name)' ec2.json
"ec2-REDACTED.compute-1.amazonaws.com"
```

Note the exit-status behaviour, which matters in shell pipelines: with no match, `first(...)`
emits **nothing at all** and still exits 0; add `-e` and it exits **4**:

```
$ jq -ce 'first(.[] | select(.state=="zzz") | .dns_name)' ec2.json ; echo $?
4
```
### 3. Robustness — the part to take away for real-world data

Your EC2 sample is homogeneous: every value is an object with every key present. **Real
output from an API is often not.** The naive idiom breaks the moment a value is not an object:

```
$ echo '{"a":{"state":"running","dns_name":"A"},"b":"just a string"}' \
| jq -c '[.[] | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]'
jq: error: Cannot index string with string ("state")
```

It aborts the whole run, rather than skipping the odd row, because `select(.state)` demands a
field of every value it sees. Two robust forms, both verified:

```
# guard the type explicitly
$ ... | jq -c '[.[] | select(type=="object") | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]'
["A",null]

# or, more tersely, pipe through the objects filter
$ ... | jq -c '[.[] | objects | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]'
["A",null]
```

`objects` (manual.md:1136-1140) yields only the objects in a stream and *silently drops*
everything else, so it is the more robust of the two — a `type=="object"` guard still has to
be written in the right place to protect every subsequent expression. A third option is the
optional operator, `.state?`, which suppresses the error on non-objects:

```
$ ... | jq -c '[.[] | .state? | select(.=="running")]'
["running"]
```
Two data-shape notes specific to your sample, both visible above:

- **`null` is a value, not an absence.** Rows whose `dns_name` is `null` still match a `state`
test and contribute a `null` to the result array (`["A",null]` above). If you want *only
real* hostnames, add `select(.dns_name != null)`.
- Your three rows only ever produced one result because exactly one is `"running"`. On a
larger fleet you would get one `dns_name` per running instance, in document order — the
document order of an object is *not* specified, so do not rely on the ordering of `.[]` over
an object. If order matters, sort explicitly (`sort_by`).
### 4. Related shapes you will hit next

```
# you have the inverse document (array of objects) and want the object-of-objects back
$ jq -c 'map({(.id): .}) | add' instances.json
$ jq -c 'INDEX(.id)' instances.json # same, via the SQL-style operator, manual.md:2514-2519

# count/group by state
$ jq -c 'map(.state) | group_by(.) | map({state: .[0], n: length})' instances.json

# transform every value in place, keeping the keys (manual.md:840-860)
$ jq -c 'map_values(.state)' ec2.json
```

`map_values(f)` is the object analogue of `map(f)`: it keeps the keys and applies `f` to each
value — the transform version of what `.[]` does for extraction. Be aware it has the same
homogeneity assumption as the naive `.[]` form: it errors if any value is not an object.

Complex assignments
Lots more things are allowed on the left-hand side of a jq assignment than
in most languages. We´ve already seen simple field accesses on the left
hand side, and it´s no surprise that array accesses work just as well:

What may come as a surprise is that the expression on the left may produce
multiple results, referring to different points in the input document:
.posts[].comments |= . + ["this is great"]

That example appends the string "this is great" to the "comments" array of
each post in the input (where the input is an object with a field "posts"
which is an array of posts).

When jq encounters an assignment like ´a = b´, it records the "path" taken
to select a part of the input document while executing a. This path is
then used to find which part of the input to change while executing the
assignment. Any filter may be used on the left-hand side of an equals -
whichever paths it selects from the input will be where the assignment is
performed.

This is a very powerful operation. Suppose we wanted to add a comment to
blog posts, using the same "blog" input above. This time, we only want to
comment on the posts written by "stedolan". We can find those posts using
the "select" function described earlier:
.posts[] | select(.author == "stedolan")

The paths provided by this operation point to each of the posts that
"stedolan" wrote, and we can comment on each of them in the same way that
we did before:

(.posts[] | select(.author == "stedolan") | .comments) |=
. + ["terrible."]

MODULES
jq has a library/module system. Modules are files whose names end in .jq.

Modules imported by a program are searched for in a default search path
(see below). The import and include directives allow the importer to alter
this path.
Paths in the a search path are subject to various substitutions.

For paths starting with ~/, the user´s home directory is substituted for
~.

For paths starting with $ORIGIN/, the directory where the jq executable is
located is substituted for $ORIGIN.

For paths starting with ./ or paths that are ., the path of the including
file is substituted for .. For top-level programs given on the com‐
mand-line, the current directory is used.

Import directives can optionally specify a search path to which the de‐
fault is appended.

The default search path is the search path given to the -L command-line
option, else ["~/.jq", "$ORIGIN/../lib/jq", "$ORIGIN/../lib"].
Null and empty string path elements terminate search path processing.

A dependency with relative path foo/bar would be searched for in
foo/bar.jq and foo/bar/bar.jq in the given search path. This is intended
to allow modules to be placed in a directory along with, for example, ver‐
sion control files, README files, and so on, but also to allow for sin‐
gle-file modules.

Consecutive components with the same name are not allowed to avoid ambigu‐
ities (e.g., foo/foo).

For example, with -L$HOME/.jq a module foo can be found in
$HOME/.jq/foo.jq and $HOME/.jq/foo/foo.jq.
If $HOME/.jq is a file, it is sourced into the main program.

import RelativePathString as NAME [<metadata>];
Imports a module found at the given path relative to a directory in a
search path. A .jq suffix will be added to the relative path string. The
module´s symbols are prefixed with NAME::.

The optional metadata must be a constant jq expression. It should be an
object with keys like homepage and so on. At this time jq only uses the
search key/value of the metadata. The metadata is also made available to
users via the modulemeta builtin.

The search key in the metadata, if present, should have a string or array
value (array of strings); this is the search path to be prefixed to the
top-level search path.

include RelativePathString [<metadata>];
Imports a module found at the given path relative to a directory in a
search path as if it were included in place. A .jq suffix will be added to
the relative path string. The module´s symbols are imported into the
caller´s namespace as if the module´s content had been included directly.

import RelativePathString as $NAME [<metadata>];
Imports a JSON file found at the given path relative to a directory in a
search path. A .json suffix will be added to the relative path string. The
file´s data will be available as $NAME::NAME.

module <metadata>;
This directive is entirely optional. It´s not required for proper opera‐

## Answer (verified with jq 1.8.2)

```
$ jq '[.[] | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]' ec2.json
[ "ec2-REDACTED.compute-1.amazonaws.com" ]
```

The reason it works is the thing you said was missing from the manual, and the manual does
in fact say it — you were looking for it in the array section.
### 1. "But there was no array. :)" — `.[]` iterates object *values* too

`.[]` is not an array operator that tolerates objects. It is documented as the **Array/Object**
Value Iterator, and the array section is simply the first half of the story:
manual.md:285 — the heading itself is `### Array/Object Value Iterator: '.[]'`

> If you use the `.[index]` syntax, but omit the index entirely, it will return *all* of the
> elements of an array. […] A filter of the form `.foo[]` is equivalent to `.foo | .[]`.
>
> **You can also use this on an object, and it will return all the values of the object.**
>
> Note that the iterator operator is a generator of values.

That last italic line is the one to internalise: **`.[]` yields values, not keys.** So on your
document it walks the three *inner objects* and hands each one to `select`, exactly as if you
had written an array by hand. Verified:

```
$ jq -c '.[] | .state' ec2.json
"running"
"terminated"
"stopped"
```

The "magic" is that `.[]` is doing the thing `to_entries` would otherwise be needed for, and
it throws the keys away. That is usually what you want here — you want the *host*, not its name.

**When you need the key as well** (e.g. to report *which* instance is running), reach for
`to_entries`, which is the same idea without the information loss — manual.md:1061-1075:

```
$ jq -c 'to_entries | map(select(.value.state=="running") | {id:.key, dns:.value.dns_name})' ec2.json
[{"id":"i-09xxxxxx","dns":"ec2-REDACTED.compute-1.amazonaws.com"}]
```
### 2. One scalar instead of an array

`select` is a filter, so it can match several values and you get an *array* of results. If you
only ever want one, wrap it in `first(...)` (manual.md:3371-3386):

```
$ jq -c 'first(.[] | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name)' ec2.json
"ec2-REDACTED.compute-1.amazonaws.com"
```

Note the exit-status behaviour, which matters in shell pipelines: with no match, `first(...)`
emits **nothing at all** and still exits 0; add `-e` and it exits **4**:

```
$ jq -ce 'first(.[] | select(.state=="zzz") | .dns_name)' ec2.json ; echo $?
4
```
### 3. Robustness — the part to take away for real-world data

Your EC2 sample is homogeneous: every value is an object with every key present. **Real
output from an API is often not.** The naive idiom breaks the moment a value is not an object:

```
$ echo '{"a":{"state":"running","dns_name":"A"},"b":"just a string"}' \
| jq -c '[.[] | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]'
jq: error: Cannot index string with string ("state")
```

It aborts the whole run, rather than skipping the odd row, because `select(.state)` demands a
field of every value it sees. Two robust forms, both verified:

```
# guard the type explicitly
$ ... | jq -c '[.[] | select(type=="object") | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]'
["A",null]

# or, more tersely, pipe through the objects filter
$ ... | jq -c '[.[] | objects | select(.state=="running") | .dns_name]'
["A",null]
```

`objects` (manual.md:1122-1130) yields only the objects in a stream and *silently drops*
everything else, so it is the more robust of the two — a `type=="object"` guard still has to
be written in the right place to protect every subsequent expression. A third option is the
optional operator, `.state?`, which suppresses the error on non-objects:

```
$ ... | jq -c '[.[] | .state? | select(.=="running")]'
["running"]
```
Two data-shape notes specific to your sample, both visible above:

- **`null` is a value, not an absence.** Rows whose `dns_name` is `null` still match a `state`
test and contribute a `null` to the result array (`["A",null]` above). If you want *only
real* hostnames, add `select(.dns_name != null)`.
- Your three rows only ever produced one result because exactly one is `"running"`. On a
larger fleet you would get one `dns_name` per running instance, in document order — the
document order of an object is *not* specified, so do not rely on the ordering of `.[]` over
an object. If order matters, sort explicitly (`sort_by`).
### 4. Related shapes you will hit next

```
# you have the inverse document (array of objects) and want the object-of-objects back
$ jq -c 'map({(.id): .}) | add' instances.json
$ jq -c 'INDEX(.id)' instances.json # same, via the SQL-style operator, manual.md:2514-2519

# count/group by state
$ jq -c 'map(.state) | group_by(.) | map({state: .[0], n: length})' instances.json

# transform every value in place, keeping the keys (manual.md:840-860)
$ jq -c 'map_values(.state)' ec2.json
```

`map_values(f)` is the object analogue of `map(f)`: it keeps the keys and applies `f` to each
value — the transform version of what `.[]` does for extraction. Be aware it has the same
homogeneity assumption as the naive `.[]` form: it errors if any value is not an object.

Important: manual.md:856-860 says `map_values` only uses `first($x|f)` — that explains the silent key deletion. Let me read it.

For any filter `f`, `map(f)` and `map_values(f)` apply `f`
to each of the values in the input array or object, that is,
to the values of `.[]`.

In the absence of errors, `map(f)` always outputs an array
whereas `map_values(f)` outputs an array if given an array,
or an object if given an object.

When the input to `map_values(f)` is an object, the output
object has the same keys as the input object except for
those keys whose values when piped to `f` produce no values
at all.

The key difference between `map(f)` and `map_values(f)` is
that the former simply forms an array from all the values of
`($x|f)` for each value, $x, in the input array or object,
but `map_values(f)` only uses `first($x|f)`.

Specifically, for object inputs, `map_value(f)` constructs
the output object by examining in turn the value of
`first(.[$k]|f)` for each key, $k, of the input. If this
expression produces no values, then the corresponding key
will be dropped; otherwise, the output object will have that
value at the key, $k.

Here are some examples to clarify the behavior of `map` and
`map_values` when applied to arrays. These examples assume the
input is `[1]` in all cases:

map_values(.+1) #=> [2]
map_values(., .) #=> [1]
map_values(empty) #=> []

`map(f)` is equivalent to `[.[] | f]` and
`map_values(f)` is equivalent to `.[] |= f`.
